title: Onsemi introduces new SiC Platform: EliteSiC M4
content: US semiconductor manufacturer Onsemi has introduced the fourth generation of its silicon carbide technology with EliteSiC M4. The new platform is set to increase power density by up to 30 per cent and reduce losses by up to 35 per cent. This could benefit, among other things, the drivetrain systems of electric vehicles.

title: Tesla FSD approved in Italy, the first big EU market to say yes
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Nov 20 2026 - 7:50 am PT
Italy’s transport ministry has granted provisional approval to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” in Europe. Italy becomes the 12th European country to allow the system, and the first of the EU’s big markets.
It also didn’t wait for Brussels. The EU committee that decides on bloc-wide recognition isn’t expected to vote until December at the earliest.
Deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini announced the decision on X on Friday. He wrote that the ministry (MIT) gave the green light after a “thorough technical feasibility check,” and that Italy is getting ahead of the EU recognition process, which he described as “still being defined.”
Tesla Europe followed with a one-liner, “Now approved in Italy, rollout begins soon,” and a video of one of its cars driving itself through Rome. There’s no firm rollout date yet.
It’s still a Level 2 driver-assist system. It can steer, brake, accelerate, and handle intersections and lane changes, but the driver has to supervise at all times and stays fully responsible for the car.
How Italy got here
The Dutch vehicle authority RDW was first,
approving FSD Supervised on April 10
under Article 39 of the EU type-approval regulation. Other member states can then recognize that approval nationally, one by one.
Ten did before Italy: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Those are mostly small markets. Together with the Netherlands, they add up to about 70 million people, or roughly 15% of the EU’s population.
Italy alone has about 59 million people, so Friday’s decision nearly doubles the share of Europeans who can legally use the system, to close to 30%.
Rome’s position moved fast. In April, Senator Carlo Calenda formally asked Salvini’s ministry to prioritize the approval. On October 29, Salvini posted that he’d had a “very positive and constructive” call with Elon Musk and that Italy supported a “swift EU approval,” which read at the time as backing for an EU-level decision, not a national one. Three weeks later, Italy went national.
A lot changed in between. Tesla
dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe
after Germany’s Transport Ministry called it misleading, and cut the maximum speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit. Then on November 16, the RDW approved
stricter driver monitoring
, including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h. That’s the version Italy is approving.
The December math gets easier
The EU’s Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV)
pushed the Tesla vote to December
after holding only discussions in October. Bloc-wide approval needs a qualified majority: at least 15 of 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU population.
Germany said in October it would back approval after Tesla agreed to the rename and the speed cap. If it follows through, Germany and the 12 approving countries would cover roughly 47% of the EU’s population.
That’s progress for Tesla, but it’s not 65%. France refused a national approval in July, and Spain hasn’t recognized the Dutch approval. Tesla needs at least one of them, plus most of the remaining holdouts.
Electrek’s Take
This is a real win for Tesla, and for Italian owners with HW4 cars who have been paying for a feature they couldn’t use at home. Italy is Tesla’s first big European market to say yes, and it shifts momentum going into December.
But it’s pretty crazy that now Europe is going to get a safer FSD than in the US.
I bet that this will get reflected in the data, if we ever get to see it.

title: Volkswagen's new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport is the electric hot hatch we want, but can't have
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Nov 20 2026 - 7:29 am PT
Volkswagen
revealed the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, an electric pocket rocket with a massive rear wing and 362 horsepower.
Will Volkswagen bring the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport to life?
We knew Volkswagen was cooking something “really spicy” up after
teasing the new GTI hot hatch
earlier this week.
Volkswagen launched the first-generation Golf GTI in 1976, which essentially defined the hot hatch. To celebrate the brand’s legendary performance badge, a signature of its sporty, practical hatchbacks, VW is entering a new era with its first fully electric GTI.
The GTI has been “one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years,” Volkswagen’s technical development boss, Kai Grünitz, said.
After opening pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, the brand’s first EV to wear the badge, Volkswagen introduced the Clubsport Concept, a souped-up two-door electric pocket rocket.
The new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept shows “how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world,” according to Grünitz.
It’s based on the production ID. Polo GTI uses the same MEB+ platform, but VW reengineered it with a larger electric motor to pump out more power.
The Clubsport is powered by a 362 hp (270 kW) front-mounted electric motor (APP550) that’s typically used in the rear of VW’s larger EVs, like
the ID. Tiguan
and the ID.7. That’s up considerably from the 233 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft of torque of the standard ID. Polo GTI offers.
Thomas Schmall, CEO of Volkswagen Group Components, said the APP550 motor is “one of the most efficient electric drives in its class.”
Thanks to an electronically controlled front differential lock (VAQ), Volkswagen said, the Clubsport version can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 4.7 seconds, beating the standard ID. Polo GTI by a full two seconds (6.8 seconds).
Volkswagen also fine-tuned the adaptive chassis control (DCC) to make it racetrack-ready and added new ceramic brakes to help slow it down.
The Clubsport version uses the same 52 kW NMC battery as the ID. Polo GTI, which can provide up to 389 hp (290 kW), Volkswagen said, enabling a top speed of 149 mph (240 km/h).
On the exterior, the Clubsport is a two-door model rather than a four-door. It’s 100 mm longer than the standard ID. Polo GTI, with each wing flared an additional 50 mm. It also gets a large motorsport splitter up front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser, and a massive carbon-fiber rear wing.
Inside, the cabin is tailored to the racetrack with a minimalist, stripped-down, two-seater layout. As such, there’s no infotainment system, just a center display to switch between drive modes.
The dash panel, side trims, and other interior elements feature dark ArtVelours microfibre with red topstitching, reinforcing the racetrack-ready interior.
Following the ID. Polo GTI, new ID.3 GTI, and Golf GTI Edition 50, the new ID. Polo Clubsport is the fourth model to debut this year under the performance badge.
Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000). In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the
ID.3 GTI
, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.
The company will showcase the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport concept car at the
Essen Motor Show
next week, starting on November 27.
Volkswagen didn’t confirm plans to launch a production version, but don’t expect it to reach the States.
The standard VW ID. Polo and GTI are not sold in the US, so the souped-up Clubsport variant likely won’t be either. Hopefully, VW changes its mind and proves us wrong.

title: Double guns: ultra-class haul truck packs dual-gun MCS charging, 4 MWh battery
content:
EV Charging
Electric Heavy Machinery
Jo Borrás
| Nov 20 2026 - 3:55 am PT
Made using AI.
NHL may not be a household name, but its all-new, all-electric NTE240E ultra-class haul track could change that with a 240 ton payload, over 4.1 MWh of battery, advanced regenerative braking, and a world’s first double-gun MCS charging setup.
For the uninitiated, Inner Mongolia North Hauler Joint Stock Co., Ltd. (NHL) is a Chinese heavy equipment manufacturer specializing in the enormous rigid-frame haul trucks used in open-pit mining operations. Established in 1988, NHL has decades of experience building mining trucks for customers around the world, including some of the industry’s largest diesel-electric hybrids. The brand’s new NTE240E is different, representing a company’s real push into battery-electric mining equipment, and it’s powering that push with some seriously ambitious technology.
Let’s start with the battery. The NTE240E packs an absolutely MASSIVE battery pack,
with the highest-capacity versions offering up to 4,100 kWh
(4.1 MWh) of onboard energy storage. Keeping that much battery topped off is no small task, which is why NHL developed an equally ambitious energy replenishment strategy supporting dual-gun MCS charging, allowing its town-sized battery to go from 20% to 90% in under an hour.
That means operators can take advantage of shift changes and scheduled rest breaks to top off the battery without sacrificing an entire work shift to charging – but even more impressive than the fact that all that juice can be crammed into so big a battery in so little time is the fact that, according to NHL, it can be done at just 25°C (about 77°F).
More than way to power up
Plugging in isn’t the only way the NTE240E drinks its juice.
NHL’s new dynamic power reception system uses overhead current collectors to supply electricity directly to the truck while it’s climbing loaded mine roads
, allowing it to then “
ride the brakes
” for more energy all the way downhill.
The combined technologies allow NHL’s operators to keep the massive trucks moving without relying entirely on their onboard batteries. The result is a claimed 15% improvement in energy efficiency over the ultra-class industry average.
That efficiency turns into savings, which means the economics of running an NTE240E could be just as compelling as the emissions savings – and those are
substantial
. NHL says each NTE240E can reduce harmful carbon emissions by more than 2,000 tons annually, even as it cuts operating costs by more than 60% compared to a comparably capable diesel.
What’s more, because the big BEV’s electrical system eliminates the need for engine-related hardware like generators and the maintenance and overhaul costs associated with those components. Taken as a whole, the NHL seems to be a compelling offering … but that’s not for me to say. You guys are the experts – let us know what you think of the new NHL NTE240E, in the comments.

title: China grid-connects world’s first artificial-cavern CAES plant - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The 300 MW/1.8 GWh project uses excavated hard-rock chambers, expanding compressed-air storage options beyond natural salt caverns.
Vincent Shaw
20 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Yuanchu No. 1 compressed air energy storage (CAES) station in Yumen, Gansu province
China’s Yuanchu No. 1 compressed air energy storage (CAES) station in Yumen, Gansu province, achieved its first grid connection on November 16, marking what its developer describes as the world’s first grid-connected CAES facility using purpose-excavated underground rock caverns.
The project was developed by China Energy Digital Technology Group, a subsidiary of China Energy Engineering Corporation, which is responsible for its investment, construction, and operation.
Rated at 300 MW/1,800 MWh, the facility is designed for an eight-hour charging cycle and six hours of continuous discharge. Total investment reached approximately CNY 2.5 billion ($368 million), with projected annual electricity generation of 600 GWh.
Its defining feature is an engineered underground air storage system. Four interconnected chambers were excavated approximately 110 meters below the surface in hard rock, creating a pressurized storage space of around 200,000 cubic meters. The system has a design pressure of 18 MPa.
The plant employs non-combustion, adiabatic CAES technology. During charging, electricity drives compressors that pressurize air, while heat generated during compression is recovered and stored. During discharge, the stored heat reheats the compressed air before expansion through turbines, eliminating the need for supplementary natural gas combustion.
According to molten-salt supplier Shandong Huayang Dier Chemical, the thermal system combines low-melting-point ternary molten salt with pressurized hot water to recover and store heat at different temperatures. Lower- and medium-temperature compression heat is stored in pressurized water tanks, while higher-temperature heat is transferred to molten-salt tanks. During discharge, both media release heat in stages to reheat the air before expansion. The developer also reports using shared heat-exchange equipment during charging and discharging, reducing equipment duplication.
The developer reports a round-trip electrical efficiency of 72%, although sustained operational data have not yet independently confirmed the figure.
The artificial-cavern approach addresses a geographical constraint on CAES deployment. Salt caverns offer relatively economical underground storage but require suitable geological formations. Excavating and sealing chambers in competent hard rock could broaden site selection, although geological conditions and construction costs remain important considerations.
Yumen lies within the Hexi Corridor, a major wind and solar development region in northwest China. The plant is intended to absorb surplus renewable electricity during off-peak periods and return it to the grid when demand rises, providing multi-hour balancing capacity.
China has been expanding its large-scale CAES fleet. At least six projects rated at 100 MW or above have been reported as grid-connected, including the 600 MW Huai’an salt-cavern station, the 700 MW Jintan Phase II project, 300 MW facilities in Yingcheng and Feicheng, the 100 MW Zhangjiakou demonstration project and Yuanchu No. 1.
According to an October 2026 report by the Energy Storage Application Branch of the China Industrial Association of Power Sources, 13 CAES projects were under construction, totaling 4.95 GW/23.95 GWh. Separately, industry figures cited in November indicated more than 36 GW of projects in preparation as of the first quarter of 2026, with nearly 100 project filings nationwide.
The figures highlight China’s growing CAES pipeline, although many proposed projects remain subject to financing, geological assessments and commercial viability. For Yuanchu No. 1, long-term efficiency, cavern integrity and operating costs will determine whether artificial-cavern technology can be replicated economically.

title: Enphase highlights new batteries, bidirectional charging - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Enphase is rolling out residential and commercial storage, meter-collared vehicle-to-grid charging, and a medium-voltage solid-state transformer.
Ryan Kennedy
20 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
Inverters
Residential
Enphase Energy is expanding its hardware lineup across home systems, commercial buildings, and high-power AI infrastructure. The company
exhibited
its new products at RE+ Las Vegas 2026.
“RE+ is where installers, developers, and utilities see the full Enphase platform in one place,” said Ken Fong, senior vice president of sales at Enphase Energy. “This year, that platform runs from the home to the commercial rooftop to data center applications and beyond, all built on the same distributed, semiconductor-based architecture.”
IQ Battery G5
The IQ Battery G5 was built to pack more home storage into a tighter, stackable footprint than earlier generations. Each 5 kWh AC-coupled module includes its own grid-forming microinverter and prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells.
Stacks scale up to 30 kWh across six blocks on a floor stand or 20 kWh across four blocks on a wall mount, with full installations scaling up to 100 kWh. Each block weighs 115.3 lbs with an IP67 enclosure, and the paired Wiring Block weighs 19.8 lbs with a NEMA-3R enclosure.
The battery carries a 15-year limited warranty, with pilots planned in Q4 2026 and volume shipments starting in Q1 2027.
IQ Bidirectional EV Charger
Enphase built the DC-based IQ Bidirectional EV Charger to let electric vehicles power a home or send energy back to the grid through a simpler meter-collar connection. It supports vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid operation and carries a 10-year limited warranty.
Pilots are expected to start in Q4 2026, followed by volume shipments in Q1 2027.
IQ Battery C80
Commercial buildings are the target for the IQ Battery C80, Enphase’s first commercial battery system, which brings modular AC-coupled storage to businesses. It gives the company an entry point into commercial peak demand charge management, backup power, and solar-plus-storage projects as residential solar growth slows.
Each enclosure delivers 80 kWh of energy capacity and scales up to 2 MWh per site. The C80 uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry with 314 Ah prismatic cells and delivers over 90% AC round-trip efficiency.
It measures 36.2 in wide, 78.7 in high, and 32.3 in deep, weighs 2,645 lbs, and operates from -22°F to 131°F. It comes in 277Y/480 V and 120Y/208 V three-phase models and carries a 15-year or 7,000-cycle warranty.
Paired with IQ9N-3P and IQ9S-3P commercial microinverters, the system stays AC-coupled to simplify installation for commercial contractors. Product pilots begin in Q1 2027, with volume shipments scheduled for Q2 2027.
IQ Solid-State Transformer (IQ SST)
AI data centers are getting a direct medium-voltage to 800 VDC power conversion path with the IQ Solid-State Transformer (IQ SST), avoiding multi-stage step-down gear. The design targets data center power bottlenecks and fast compute load swings, while domestic module production in Arlington, Texas supports U.S. manufacturing goals against established industrial power rivals.
It converts 13.8 kV and 34.5 kV medium-voltage AC directly to 800 VDC, supporting both 800 VDC and ±400 VDC rack architectures. Each power module is rated at 5.5 kW with over 98.5% peak efficiency expected, a 250–500 kHz switching frequency, a custom 22 nm Kestrel control ASIC, and gallium nitride (GaN) power switching, weighing roughly 8 lbs with silicone potting.
Racks scale up to 5 MW with ambient-air cooling and up to 1,008 power modules in a delta configuration for AC/DC operation (or 1,008 AC/DC plus 672 DC/DC modules), while skids scale up to 10 MW. The modular hot-swap design targets 99.999% availability, sub-millisecond transient response, and a 10-year limited warranty.
Enphase demonstrated 13.8 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion in October 2026 and expects full-system demonstrations to finish by the end of 2026. Customer pilots are slated for 2027, followed by initial commercial shipments in 2028.
Additional hardware and software
Residential and commercial IQ9N microinverters, the IQ Meter Collar, the IQ Combiner 6C, and the upcoming IQ System Controller 4 round out home and commercial installations.
Other additions include the IQ EV Charger 2, an AC-based bidirectional charging option, the U.S. IQ Plugin Solar System, and the Enphase Air smart thermostat. Solargraf software also features unified residential and commercial workflows with built-in AI tools.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: China starts operating 195 km hydrogen pipeline - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, ACME Group has approved a $3.6 billion green ammonia project in India, while researchers in Chile have assessed hydrogen production from curtailed renewable power. Qair has inaugurated a hydrogen plant in France, Plug Power has launched a utility-scale electrolyzer offering, and Protium has advanced two UK hydrogen projects.
Sergio Matalucci
20 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Hydrogen
Utility-scale
has started operating a 195 km hydrogen pipeline connecting Darhan Muminggan United Banner with Baotou, Inner Mongolia, reported Xinhua News Agency. The pipeline has an approved annual transport capacity of 100,000 tons of hydrogen, potentially increasing to 240,000 tons. Developed by Inner Mongolia Huadian Huameng Pipeline, the infrastructure will connect renewable hydrogen production facilities in northern Baotou with industrial consumers in the south. Pipeline transport could reduce hydrogen delivery costs from about CNY 13 ($1.83)/kg by tube trailer to approximately CNY 3/kg, according to Xinhua. China has been
expanding its hydrogen transport infrastructure
to connect renewable energy resources with industrial demand.
ACME Group
has reached a final investment decision (FID) on a $3.6 billion green ammonia project in Odisha, India, with an annual production capacity of 760,000 tons. The facility, scheduled for commissioning in 2029, will feature a 2,200-ton-per-day ammonia production loop designed by Thyssenkrupp Uhde. It will use renewable electricity to produce hydrogen through electrolysis for green ammonia production, targeting customers in India, Japan and Europe. Brookfield has committed up to $600 million to support ACME’s green molecules platform. The project is expected to avoid more than 1.5 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually. ACME has also
secured green ammonia supply contracts in India
and is developing green methanol projects.
Researchers in Chile
have found that green hydrogen produced from curtailed solar electricity could achieve a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) as low as $5.58/kg, compared with $7.27/kg for the most competitive wind projects. The study, “
Green hydrogen from curtailment: Real data analysis
,” assessed operational data from 56 solar plants and 44 wind farms with a combined capacity of 10.4 GW between July 2023 and June 2024. Curtailment occurred in about 25% of recorded hourly intervals, predominantly at low power levels. Using a techno-economic model based on proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzers, the researchers identified optimal electrolyzer capacities of 5% to 13% of the renewable plants’ net effective power across the 10 best-performing projects, all located in northern Chile. The projects achieved LCOH values of $5.58/kg to $6.97/kg, with electrolyzer capacity factors of 25% to 30%. Deviations of up to 50% from optimal electrolyzer sizing increased hydrogen production costs by no more than 3.8%. The study, to be published in
Energy Reports
, found that curtailed renewable electricity could support competitive hydrogen production, although storage, compression and transport costs remain additional considerations. Chile has
experienced significant renewable energy curtailment
, particularly at solar plants in the north of the country.
has inaugurated its Hyd’Occ renewable hydrogen production facility in Occitanie, France. The 20 MW plant is supported by a regional network of hydrogen refueling stations forming part of the European H2 Corridor. Qair
opened its first hydrogen refueling stations in Béziers and Narbonne
in spring 2026. A second development phase will double the plant’s installed capacity to 40 MW, increasing annual hydrogen production capacity to 5,400 tons. Total investment amounts to €130 million.
Plug Power
has launched GenEco Scale, an integrated electrolyzer plant offering for utility-scale hydrogen production. Arcadia eFuels has selected the system for a 280 MW hydrogen facility at its Project ARC development in Texas. Plug Power said it has completed the project’s technical evaluation and front-end engineering design (FEED) study. Once operational, the facility is expected to support production of approximately 23.2 million gallons of electro-sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) annually. Plug Power previously
signed a 280 MW electrolyzer supply agreement with Arcadia eFuels
for a separate project in Denmark.
has completed due diligence for two green hydrogen projects under the UK government’s second Hydrogen Allocation Round (HAR2). The South Tees Net Zero project in northern England and the South Wales Net Zero project have both advanced to the Invitation to Offer stage. The 70 MW South Tees facility is designed to produce up to 11,000 tons of green hydrogen annually, equivalent to about 433 GWh, for industrial consumers in Teesside. The projects will now progress toward Low Carbon Hydrogen Agreements, which provide revenue support to reduce investment risks. Protium is also
developing other UK hydrogen projects
, including a 15 MW electrolyzer project that secured support under the first Hydrogen Allocation Round.

title: Proper Voltage, Unigrid unveil sodium-ion storage solution for data centers - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Salt Vault High Power cabinet aims to deliver some of the benefits of sodium-ion chemistries including the concept that rapid and repeated power transients may not degrade sodium-ion batteries as fast as lithium and lead-acid.
Tristan Rayner
20 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Energy Storage
California-based duo Proper Voltage and Unigrid have teamed up to pair voltage-control electronics with sodium-chromium oxide cells to create a 73.1 kWh backup cabinet aimed at delivering power to data centers.
Battery integration firm Proper Voltage announced that it has launched Salt Vault, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery cabinet built around sodium-ion cells from San Diego-based
. Commercial deliveries to unnamed early-adopter data center and critical infrastructure operators are scheduled to begin in April 2027.
The system combines Proper Voltage’s software that it calls its battery operating system (bOS) with Unigrid’s sodium-chromium oxide (NCO) chemistry.
According to Proper Voltage’s product specifications, the Salt Vault High Power cabinet delivers 73.1 kWh of capacity and 333 kW of power output at a nominal 522 VDC, rated for 10,000 cycles. It operates across a discharge temperature range of -20 C to 40 C and a charge range of 0 C to 40 C. A single module in the cabinet is 6.1 kWh.
The two companies are targeting a specific operational problem in AI data centers, where training and inference clusters swing from idle to peak load in milliseconds. Those repeated power transients may accelerate degradation in conventional lead-acid and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) backup batteries.
Proper Voltage says its software-defined voltage control as part of its bOS regulates output across the full state of charge, allowing the sodium-ion cabinet to drop into existing UPS architectures without inverter redesigns. It can also adapt to 800 V racks, as the industry scales towards that voltage level.
No independent performance data or pricing has been disclosed.
“Performance is what drives the best models, and the battery behind them must be resilient and adaptive across every one of those demands,” said Charlie Welch, CEO of Proper Voltage. Unigrid CEO Darren Tan said the NCO chemistry is built for high-rate pulse power and thermal stability under heavy cycling.
The launch adds to a growing push by sodium-ion developers into AI infrastructure, where fire safety and high-rate discharge may matter more than energy density.
Earlier this year,
Energy Vault locked in 1.5 GWh of Peak Energy’s sodium-ion systems
for its AI data center portfolio.
And, less happily, ESS Tech introduced a
modular sodium-ion platform for the same market
in July, before it went out of business in November.
The hill to climb towards supplying hyperscalers is steep.
Nvidia’s BESS qualification program only Tesla, LG, and Hitachi,
underscoing how hard supply deals are for tier-one data center contracts.

政策分类依据: EVN发布决定，规定屋顶光伏并网的技术规范与验收程序，属于公平接入的技术标准要求
content: Vietnam’s state-owned national power utility Vietnam Electricity (EVN) has introduced new technical requirements and acceptance procedures for rooftop solar installations that export surplus electricity to the grid. Decision No. 1382/QĐ-EVN , issued on November 18, sets out technical specifications and a process for testing and accepting rooftop solar installations connected to EVN’s monitoring, data-collection and control systems. It replaces Decision No. 378/QĐ-EVN, issued on Mar. 12, 2025, and takes effect immediately. The requirements cover rooftop solar systems designed for self-consumption that export surplus electricity to the grid and fall within the electricity company’s monitoring and control remit. Under the specifications, installations must transmit operational data to the electricity company’s monitoring system, with inverter output updated at intervals of no more than five minutes. Systems must also be capable of both receiving and executing remote commands to limit exported power, as well as automatically adjusting inverter output to comply with instructions from the utility. The acceptance testing procedure includes documentation reviews, site inspections, communications testing and verification of monitoring and control signals. Utilities must also test a system’s ability to reduce exports in response to power limitation commands and check its behaviour during communications outages and faults before issuing any acceptance documentation. EVN says system owners are responsible for installing compatible monitoring, metering and communications equipment, providing technical documentation and coordinating with utilities during testing. Electricity companies are responsible for providing connection and communications configurations, verifying cybersecurity and monitoring functionality and conducting the acceptance tests. The decision comes as Vietnam looks to accelerate rooftop solar deployment. The Vietnamese government ordered provinces to speed up rooftop solar support policies in September. Last month, it called on provincial and municipal authorities to introduce these policies by the end of the year . A Ministry of Industry and Trade publication released in September also outlined plans to link distributed rooftop solar, behind-the-meter battery energy storage systems and electric vehicles into flexible grid assets , moving away from basic time-of-use tariffs. Vietnam’s solar capacity surpassed 19 GW by the end of 2025, with around 586 MW of solar added last year. The country had more than 11.45 GW of rooftop solar capacity across 134,410 installations as of the end of August 2026, according to figures from EVN. title: High pressure drives irradiance gains across South East Asia as Sichuan misses out - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
In a new weekly update for pv magazine,
, a DNV company, reports that October 2026 saw solar irradiance exceed average levels by over 20% across southern China and Southeast Asia, driven by strong El Niño conditions, persistent high pressure, and reduced cloud cover. However, cloudiness in Sichuan and Chongqing, cold fronts, Typhoon Champi, and wildfire haze in Indonesia reduced solar irradiance in some areas.
20 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
October 2026 brought unusually sunny conditions across much of southern China and mainland South East Asia, with irradiance 20%+ above average in the strongest-affected areas, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Persistent high pressure over South East Asia and the South China Sea, alongside a very strong El Niño, suppressed rainfall and cloud. Sichuan and Chongqing missed much of the irradiance boost, while repeated cold fronts and Typhoon Champi interrupted the broader pattern farther north and east.
The strongest positive irradiance anomalies stretched across Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan, through northern Indochina and into the Philippines. Rainfall was up to 6 millimeters per day below average across much of the same region, helping keep skies clearer. October rainfall in the
southern southwest was more than 50% below normal, with drought persisting in Yunnan, southwest Guizhou and southern Guangxi. Southern and central China were also more than 1.5 C warmer than average. Hong Kong recorded its warmest October, with a mean temperature of 27.6 C. A weaker
northeast monsoon and persistent high pressure helped limit the usual influx of moisture and cloud, reinforcing the sunnier pattern during a very strong El Niño.
Sichuan and Chongqing were a notable exception. While surrounding regions recorded positive irradiance anomalies, the basin saw slightly below-average irradiance for October. More easterly winds than usual and lower pressure over the Sichuan Basin helped keep cloud concentrated over the region, with the surrounding terrain and anomalously high pressure limiting its dispersal. The additional cloud coincided with neutral to slightly above-average rainfall in October, in contrast with the drier conditions surrounding the basin and farther south.
Farther north and east, repeated cold-air outbreaks brought periods of increased cloud and precipitation, interrupting the otherwise favourable irradiance conditions. China experienced six cold-air outbreaks during October, 2.4 more than average. These brought rain and snow across parts of northern and eastern China, with eastern Hebei and most of Beijing receiving 50–100 mm of precipitation from 15–23 October.
Typhoon Champi provided another interruption to the broader pattern. The storm formed on 11 October and reached winds near 215 km/h, affecting Taiwan, Japan and China. Cloud and rainfall associated with the system reduced irradiance as it moved through the region, with 62,400 people evacuated in Shanghai due to the conditions. October was particularly active for tropical weather overall, with eight tropical cyclones across the South China Sea and western North Pacific during the month.
Farther south, Sumatra and Kalimantan recorded below-average irradiance despite substantial rainfall deficits. Indonesia had recorded more than 1.06 million fire hotspots by 14 October, with widespread smoke and haze reducing incoming sunlight despite the otherwise dry conditions. Aerosol optical depth shows where the heaviest concentrations of smoke and haze occurred during the month.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: Mexico's solar capacity could reach 43.8 GW by 2035 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
GlobalData has raised its solar growth forecast for Mexico by 6 GW, citing a growing pipeline of renewable energy projects. However, grid congestion, transmission constraints and regulatory uncertainty could slow deployment.
Luis Ini
20 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
The Villanueva PV plant in Mexico
Mexico’s installed solar capacity is expected to increase from 13.7 GW in 2025 to 43.8 GW by 2035, according to the latest report on the Mexican electricity market by research and consultancy firm GlobalData. The firm forecasts that renewables will account for 42.3% of the country’s total installed power capacity by 2035, up from 22.9% in 2025.
The latest projection represents an upward revision of 6 GW from GlobalData’s December 2025 forecast, which put Mexico’s installed solar capacity at 37.8 GW by 2035.
The Mexico Power Market Trends and Analysis by Capacity, Generation, Transmission, Distribution, Regulations, Key Players and Forecast to 2035 report projects that Mexico’s total installed power capacity will increase from 104.2 GW in 2025 to 156 GW in 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate of 4.1%. Over the same period, natural gas-fired generation capacity is expected to rise from 53.4 GW to 64.8 GW.
Despite the expansion of renewables, GlobalData expects thermal power plants to continue accounting for nearly 60% of Mexico’s electricity generation in 2035, while the share of renewables in the generation mix is projected to increase from 14.5% to 31.9%. The consultancy also forecasts that electricity consumption will rise from 328.5 TWh in 2025 to 423.2 TWh in 2035, driven by industrial nearshoring, the expansion of data centers, and growing demand for air conditioning.
Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, a power sector analyst at GlobalData, said the 2025 Electricity Sector Law and the binding nature of the 2025-2039 Electricity Sector Development Plan (PLADESE) have reshaped Mexico’s investment landscape. The new framework guarantees the state at least 54% of the electricity injected into the grid and gives a central role to mixed-investment projects involving the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) and private companies.
Against this backdrop, the Mexican government announced in June its target of adding 22 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. The Ministry of Energy (Sener) recently reported the selection of 121 solar and wind projects totaling 18 GW. Meanwhile, CFE has increased planned investment in its portfolio of mixed-capital renewable energy projects to $10.6 billion. The portfolio includes 8,026 MW of generation capacity and more than 2,500 MW of energy storage capacity.
GlobalData has identified a pipeline of power generation projects exceeding 45 GW, dominated by solar PV. However, it warned that transmission and distribution losses, estimated at around 11.5%, and congestion on transmission lines connecting northern Mexico with demand centers in central Mexico and the Bajío region could slow the connection of new projects to the grid.
“Mexico is not lacking in projects or resources. The pace of the transition will depend on whether the mixed-investment model can attract international developers – following years of regulatory uncertainty – and on whether the CFE can expand transmission infrastructure quickly enough,” said Saibasan.

title: China's TOPCon solar module export prices slip as makers clear low-efficiency stock ahead of new standard - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides a quick look at the main price trends in the global PV industry.
20 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Free-On-Board (FOB) China mainstream module prices edged lower this week, weighed down by continued price weakness in lower-efficiency modules, as manufacturers clear inventories ahead of a stricter module efficiency standard taking effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
According to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Nov. 17, the Chinese Module Marker (CMM), the OPIS benchmark assessment for TOPCon modules below 645 W from China, fell 0.93% on the week to $0.106/W FOB China, after five consecutive weeks unchanged at $0.107/W.
Forward prices for Q1 2027 loading tracked the weakness in the spot module market, falling 0.93% week on week to $0.106/W, while Q2 through Q4 2027 held steady at $0.105/W.
Across efficiency grades, price indications for high-efficiency TOPCon modules, defined as products above 650 W, were heard in the low $0.110s/W, while back-contact modules were heard in the low-to-mid $0.110s/W. By contrast, a Dow Jones Energy market survey showed that lower-efficiency TOPCon modules, particularly those in the 625-630 W range, were quoted in the low $0.100s/W on an FOB China basis, with prices in some regions already falling below $0.100/W.
Industry sources noted that manufacturers have stepped up inventory clearance efforts in the fourth quarter, anticipating weaker domestic offtake for lower-efficiency modules once the new standard comes into effect. Under the standard, the minimum efficiency for TOPCon modules sold in China will be 23.2%, corresponding to a power output of 630 W.
Major producers’ inventories of lower-efficiency modules are already running low, one leading manufacturer said, as most have shifted production lines toward higher-efficiency products and average module power ratings among major TOPCon producers have reached around 640 W. Most of the remaining lower-efficiency stock sits with smaller or tier-2 players, who are undercutting prices aggressively, the manufacturer said.
A top-tier integrated module manufacturer said aggressive discounting in the lower-efficiency segment has also placed downward pressure on mainstream module prices, as procurement teams increasingly use lower-priced offers as leverage in price negotiations. The manufacturer added that while policies aimed at curbing module oversupply and regulating prices could support the market over the longer term, intense price competition among manufacturers is likely to persist in the near term.
Meanwhile, a divergence between domestic and export module prices has become increasingly evident since the start of Q4 2026.
Domestic mainstream TOPCon module prices have softened amid weakening demand, while export prices have remained comparatively resilient, with market sources noting that manufacturers’ quotations for overseas markets have largely resisted the downward trend in domestic prices.
According to OPIS data, EXW China TOPCon module prices fell by more than 1.8% since the beginning of October, while FOB China TOPCon mainstream modules remained broadly unchanged, before edging down by 0.93% this week.
In domestic tenders, China Energy Engineering Corporation (CEEC) shortlisted 23 bidders for its 2026 centralized module procurement tender, covering 15 GW of TOPCon, heterojunction (HJT) and back-contact modules. TOPCon modules accounted for the largest share at 10.7 GW, with shortlisted bids of CNY 0.695-0.770 ($0.104-0.115)/W. Back-contact modules represented 3.3 GW, with six companies shortlisted and bids of CNY 0.760-0.779/W, while HJT modules accounted for the remaining 1 GW, with bids of CNY 0.717-0.752/W.
OPIS is a specialist business within Dow Jones Energy, a global energy intelligence business that brings together trusted price reporting, research and market intelligence across the energy value chain. OPIS publishes the
OPIS Global Solar Markets Service
, which includes pricing data for solar panels and components across Asia, Europe and the U.S., manufacturing capacity data, module forward curves, and a global solar policy tracker.

title: Video: New underwater robot dives 328 feet deep to spot hull damage
content: A Chinese underwater robot that lets boat owners inspect propellers, check hull damage, and explore submerged areas without getting wet is now available for $3,499.Developed by underwater robotics specialist QYSEA, the FIFISH V6 EXPERT is a tethered remotely operated vehicle (ROV) with a modular design that includes detachable components for its motor, lighting, camera, and battery.The system combines 4K cameras, multidirectional movement, and an optional robotic arm to capture footage and handle small objects underwater. The system allows users to investigate potential damage, check for tangled ropes, and examine submerged objects from the surface. Robotic diving expertDesigned to operate in environments that are difficult or unsafe for divers to access, the ROV combines a high-definition camera, six degrees of freedom (6-DOF) movement, powerful LED lighting, and compatibility with several underwater tools. It can descend to depths of up to 100 meters (328 feet), allowing users to examine boat hulls, propellers, underwater structures, and other submerged objects.The robot measures 38.3 centimeters long, 33.1 centimeters wide, and 14.3 centimeters high. It weighs approximately 4.6 kilograms (10.14 pounds), making it relatively compact for transportation and deployment. Its propulsion system uses multiple thrusters to provide movement in six directions: forward and backward, left and right, and up and down. It can also rotate through 360 degrees in yaw, pitch, and roll, allowing it to change orientation without needing to turn around. QYSEA lists its maximum speed at 3 knots (1.5 meters per second).The V6 EXPERT uses a 1/2.3-inch Sony CMOS image sensor with 12-megapixel resolution and an f/2.5 lens. Its camera offers a 166-degree field of view above water and a 96-degree field of view underwater. It can record 4K video at 25 or 30 frames per second, while 1080p footage can be captured at up to 120 frames per second. To improve visibility in dark underwater environments, the ROV carries two LED lights producing a combined 6,000 lumens. The lights have a 5,500K color temperature and a 120-degree beam angle. Users can save footage and photographs using its removable microSD storage system, which comes with a 128GB card and supports cards up to 256GB according to QYSEA’s current specifications.Precision diving technologyThe robot also incorporates onboard sensors to help maintain its position and orientation underwater. These include a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, depth sensor, and temperature sensor. According to the firm, its depth-lock function can maintain a selected depth with an accuracy of approximately ±1 centimeter, helping the vehicle remain steady while inspecting a particular section of a boat or underwater structure. Other intelligent features include Vision Lock, Diver Tracking, and Q-STEADY 2.0 stabilization technology. Arm+1Power comes from a 156Wh battery, with an operating duration of approximately one to four hours depending on working conditions. QYSEA also advertises fast charging, with the battery reaching 90 percent capacity in about an hour, although actual charging times can vary. An optional Onshore Power Supply System (OPSS) allows extended operations using a surface-based power source rather than relying entirely on the onboard battery.The V6 EXPERT connects to its surface controller through a tether cable available in 100-meter (328-foot) and 200-meter (656-foot) configurations. The cable has a tensile strength of 100 kilogram-force and neutral buoyancy underwater, helping prevent it from pulling the vehicle down or interfering with its movement. The remote controller uses 5GHz Wi-Fi connectivity and offers up to four hours of operating time.One of its most useful features is the Q-IF interface, which supports additional equipment for different underwater tasks. Compatible accessories include a robotic arm with parallel grippers for retrieving objects, a retrieval hook, a 2D imaging sonar for locating objects in poor visibility, and measurement tools such as laser scalers and distance meters. Water-quality sensors can also measure dissolved oxygen, salinity, turbidity, and pH. For boat owners, the robotic arm is particularly useful for handling small objects, while the camera provides a closer look at damaged or obstructed areas. However, the robot’s capabilities depend on the accessories fitted and underwater conditions.

title: The Next Phase of Robotics: From Technological Progress to Real-World Impact
content: Robotics is entering a new stage of development. Advances in AI and embodied intelligence are enabling machines to perceive, reason, and interact with the physical world in increasingly sophisticated ways. Yet the range of tasks robots can reliably perform remains limited, while many capabilities already available have yet to reach widespread commercial adoption.Pudu Robotics is working to close that gap between what robots can demonstrate and what businesses can put to work. Following the October opening of its European headquarters in Neuss, Germany, the company gathered regional partners in Amsterdam on November 4, 2026, for its European Partner Summit. To date, Pudu has shipped over 130,000 units across more than 85 countries and regions, deploying machines across 16 industries and over 900 application scenarios.Felix Zhang, CEO and founder of Pudu Robotics, sees two priorities for the industry. Advances in embodied intelligence can expand the range of tasks robots can perform, while simpler deployment can help businesses put existing capabilities to work.Why real-world deployment demands multiple robot formsControlled demonstrations often highlight single, general-purpose humanoid robots.  Real workplaces, however, involve a wide range of tasks, environments, and operational requirements. A robot designed for floor cleaning, for example, has different hardware and functional requirements from one built to transport materials or interact with people.Pudu Robotics addresses these varied needs through six product lines. They cover service delivery, commercial cleaning, industrial delivery, general embodied AI, commercial lawn care, and residential lawn care. Expanding its footprint from indoor commercial spaces to outdoor environments and home use, the portfolio ranges from the newly announced PUDU TOMO S Series—the company’s first consumer robotics product—to professional outdoor solutions such as the PUDU GT Series commercial lawn mowers.In Switzerland, supermarket chain Denner started with a four-store pilot and later scaled to 200 PUDU CC1 four-in-one cleaning robots for routine floor maintenance. At St. Antonius Hospital in the Netherlands, five different Pudu models—the CC1, FlashBot, SwiftBot, MT1, and T300—handle separate jobs ranging from floor cleaning to moving pathological samples and internal supplies. Austria’s Parkhotel splits up daily tasks much the same way. It runs five models across restaurant delivery, room service, front-desk reception, and cleaning. Across Europe, Pudu Robotics also serves major operators including EDEKA, Carrefour, Marriott, and Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport.One Brain, Multiple EmbodimentsTo build a common intelligence foundation across different robot types and expand task coverage, Pudu Robotics developed its One Brain, Multiple Embodiments architecture. This framework provides a shared technological foundation for specialized service robots, quadrupeds like the PUDU D5, semi-humanoids like the PUDU D7, and full humanoids like the PUDU D9.Two proprietary technologies form the core of this system: PuduFM and PuduAgent. PuduFM is an embodied intelligence foundation model built around spatial understanding, physical reasoning, and future-state prediction. It fuses multi-sensor data from vision, LiDAR, and inertial measurement units.PuduAgent acts as a universal embodied AI agent platform that interprets high-level user goals and breaks them down into executable physical actions.. Together, PuduFM and PuduAgent support embodied navigation, manipulation, and interaction. Pudu Robotics is also exploring Vision-Language Navigation (VLN), which combines visual perception with language-based understanding to further enhance autonomous navigation and environmental adaptability. By significantly reducing deployment complexity and costs, this approach moves robots closer to out-of-the-box readiness, reduces development overhead, and enhances generalization across varied environments with less reliance on fixed routes or specific site configurations—ultimately helping accelerate the commercial penetration of Pudu’s robots across diverse business scenarios.Scaling commercialization through local infrastructureSustained commercial adoption requires more than capable hardware and software. Companies also need localized training, maintenance, and reliable supply chains. In Europe, Pudu operates in more than 20 countries and has recorded over 60% average annual growth across the past two years.Its new European headquarters in Neuss brings offices, product demonstrations, training, sales, after-sales support, and repair under one roof. Nearly 50 sales professionals and nearly 40 technical support staff run these regional operations, backed by warehouses in Germany and the Netherlands. This local hub acts as an operational anchor to deepen regional service capabilities and support long-term adoption.Industry rankings reflect this commercial reach. Frost & Sullivan ranks Pudu first globally in commercial service robotics by both revenue and shipments. Counterpoint Research’s August 2026 report also placed the company first globally in commercial cleaning robot shipments and revenue.As robotics advances, progress will depend not only on what machines can do, but also on how effectively those capabilities can be applied across different tasks and operating environments. Pudu Robotics’ combination of specialized robot forms, shared embodied AI technologies, and regional support infrastructure offers one example of how the industry is working toward that goal.Visit Pudu Robotics for more on its commercial robotics portfolio and embodied AI architecture.

title: US researchers built open-source chip for smarter wearable devices
content: Researchers at the New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) and collaborating institutions have developed an open-source microcontroller that combines sensing, wireless connectivity, onboard storage, and battery management into a device about the size of a quarter, opening the door to compact wearables, robotic systems, and other connected electronics.They named it TinZr (pronounced “TIN-zer”), which is the square-shaped microcontroller that measures just 0.98 inches (2.5 centimeters) on each side. Despite its compact footprint, it integrates an inertial measurement unit (IMU) for tracking motion and orientation, a microSD card reader for local data storage, a battery management circuit, and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity.Researchers positioned TinZr as a flexible, open-source system that can be adapted for a range of applications covering physiological monitoring to robotics and industrial sensing.Built to simplify wearable electronicsMicrocontrollers act as the central processing units of many embedded devices that can collect information from sensors, store data, and communicate with other electronics. However, combining all of these functions into a compact board often requires engineers to compromise on size or capability.According to the researchers, the chip was designed to overcome those limitations by integrating multiple functions into a single miniature platform without significantly increasing its footprint. Besides keeping it tiny, the the microcontroller has wireless connectivity; the board supports analog, digital, and serial communication interfaces through general-purpose input/output (GPIO) pins. Together, these features could let developers connect a wide variety of external sensors.Lead author Ludvik Alkhoury, who completed his doctoral research at NJIT and is now a postdoctoral associate at Weill Cornell Medicine, said the team could not find an existing microcontroller that combined the required size, form factor, and functionality.“You couldn’t find anything on the market that has the same size, same form factor, and also has all the functionalities that we wanted,” Alkhoury said.The project originated while researchers were developing a wearable oximeter for the U.S. Navy to monitor pilots’ heart rate and blood oxygen levels amid high-speed maneuvers that can cause pilots to lose consciousness. Those strict size and weight constraints ultimately led the team to design an even smaller and more versatile electronics platform.Designed as flexible research platformWith onboard battery management, wireless communications, and removable storage, TinZr can continuously collect data from attached sensors without relying on external hardware. The researchers described it as a general-purpose data acquisition platform that can be customized for many different scientific and engineering projects.Potential applications could go far beyond wearable health monitors. The team envisions the device monitoring brain activity in laboratory animals, measuring movement and physical strain in construction workers. They also hope to use the device to coordinate swarms of drones and support robotics research that requires compact, low-power electronics.The researchers have made the quarter-sized controller fully open source to encourage wider adoption. Its Arduino software library is available on GitHub, while printed circuit board designs, component lists, and 3D-printable enclosure files are available through the Zenodo research repository. This allows engineers to modify both the hardware and software to suit specialized applications.Rather than targeting a single use case, the developers hope TinZr will form a foundation for new wearable technologies, sensor platforms, and robotic systems that benefit from combining wireless communication, onboard storage, and sensor integration in a compact, customizable package.The researcher described the platform in the journal HardwareX.

title: Phantom MKII: Foundation unveils 2nd-gen battlefield humanoid robot
content: San Francisco-based robotics startup Foundation Future Industries has unveiled its second-generation humanoid robot, the Phantom MKII, alongside an upgraded artificial intelligence control system called Cortex II. Engineered for heavy industrial work and military support roles, the new bipedal platform is designed to haul up to 200 pounds (91 kilograms) while walking through rain, snow, and dust.Founded in 2024 by CEO Sankaet Pathak and former U.S. Marine Corps officer Mike LeBlanc, Foundation has positioned itself differently from competitors focused solely on indoor warehouse or factory automation. While most commercial humanoids operate in controlled environments, Foundation has explicitly pursued dual-use defense and rugged field applications, aiming to begin early production of the MKII in the San Francisco Bay Area in early 2027.Weatherproofing, payload gains, and Cortex IIAccording to an interview with Pathak published by Fast Company on November 18, 2026, the Phantom MKII directly addresses hardware bottlenecks uncovered during early field trials of its predecessor, the Phantom MK-1. Earlier testing highlighted limitations in battery runtime, waterproofing, and lifting capacity. These constraints restricted how long the first-generation robot could operate outdoors.To overcome those hurdles, engineers redesigned the Phantom MKII with environmental sealing against precipitation and dust, higher-load actuators capable of supporting a 200-pound walking payload, and a simplified assembly that Pathak claims cuts the bill-of-materials cost in half. On the software side, the companion Cortex II control system is built to learn physical tasks by observing human demonstrations, requiring as few as 60 examples for certain operations rather than extensive custom programming.Lessons from Ukraine trials and battlefield philosophyThe hardware overhaul follows Foundation’s high-profile push to test humanoid robotics in active conflict zones. Earlier in 2026, the company drew widespread attention after sending two Phantom MK-1 units to Ukraine for non-combat logistics and reconnaissance evaluations, though independent reporting later noted disagreements over how extensively the prototypes operated on the ground. Those trials reinforced the need for fall recovery, ruggedized joints, and longer endurance before humanoids can handle frontline supply runs or hazard detection. Unlike robotics developers that strictly prohibit military uses, Foundation openly embraces defense deployment under a “human-in-the-loop” framework, meaning human operators retain final authority over any use of force. In his interview with Fast Company, Pathak noted that while current defense work focuses on logistics rather than direct combat, the company would consider arming its robots if the U.S. military requested it. “I don’t think you can build a utopia and then not defend it,” Pathak said, outlining a broader vision in which robot fleets handle dangerous labor across construction, mining, and national security.Manufacturing ambitions amid financial headwindsDespite the technical upgrades showcased in the Phantom MKII, Foundation faces significant execution tests before its 2027 production target. As reported by CNBC and 36Kr, the startup recently experienced cash-flow pressures, including a missed staff payroll in late October 2026, while questions remain over how quickly its early military research agreements will convert into large-scale procurement orders. Whether the Phantom MKII can deliver its claimed 200-pound payload and outdoor durability in independent testing will determine if Foundation can turn its dual-use defense thesis into fielded hardware.

title: China’s new robot upgrades 98-foot live power line in just 15 minutes
content: Humans climbing up electric poles to carry out repair work could soon be a thing of the past in China.That shift may be closer than expected, thanks to robots developed by the state-owned power supply company in Jiangsu province.State Grid Changzhou Power Supply Company recently demonstrated the technology, in which robots placed insulating material on live overhead power lines without turning off the electricity.By allowing maintenance to be carried out while the grid remained energized, the installation did not require shutting down the power supply, providing residents with seamless electricity as the upgrade work was ongoing.Safely sleeving power linesAccording to the company, the newly developed robots, which weigh a little more than 65 pounds (less than 30 kilograms), completed the task of sleeving a 30-meter power line in just 15 minutes.The Chinese power supplier said the robots could be adapted to upgrade power distribution networks of 35 kilovolts (kV) and below, potentially extending the technology to a wider range of maintenance projects.To carry out the task, the robot can automatically access power lines, position itself using its machine vision feature, and accurately move and position the insulating sleeve before installation using its servo motors. At the same time, the machine is well protected from the strong electromagnetic environment, steering clear of any electrical shock.Human operator aids deploymentAlthough the robot performs most of the physical work on its own, it does not operate entirely without human involvement.A human operator remains on the ground and controls or supervises the robot using a remote-control device, computer, or control console.Once remotely deployed by an operator, the robot autonomously travels along energized power lines, installs insulating sleeves with precise alignment, and uses onboard sensors to verify installation quality in real time.According to the company, the pilot was conducted safely without affecting electricity use for consumers. Moreover, a later on-site inspection of the power lines showed that the sleeves were installed securely and met the required docking accuracy, meaning each sleeve was correctly connected, the company said in its press statement.Edge over manual maintenanceThe successful demonstration also highlighted the broader advantages of replacing conventional maintenance methods with robotic systems.The company said the exercise shows the equipment effectively avoids the safety risks of high-altitude work while preventing power outages, suggesting a shift away from traditional insulation upgrades that rely heavily on manual pole climbing and bucket truck operations. Moreover, such conventional methods are often unsuitable for residential areas with narrow alleys and also pose additional safety risks.Building on those results, the company advocated the use of these automated robots at construction sites where bucket trucks may have difficulty reaching, allowing maintenance work to be completed more safely and efficiently without interrupting electricity supply.Earlier this year, power utilities in southwestern China deployed robotic snakes to inspect power lines and help ensure a stable electricity supply.The snake-like robots wrap around power lines and use onboard cameras and sensors to detect hazards such as damaged wires, worn components, and abnormal temperatures.According to online media reports, these robots inspected more than 80 miles (130 kilometers) of distribution lines serving exam sites near airport no-fly zones.

title: 250-mile US corridor planned for hypersonic, supersonic flight tests
content: A 250-mile stretch of airspace between Texas and New Mexico could become a dedicated test corridor for supersonic and hypersonic flights under a proposal backed by four US organizations. The route would connect Midland International Air & Space Port in West Texas with Spaceport America in southern New Mexico, giving researchers a place to measure sonic booms and study how high-speed flights could fit into civilian air traffic.The partners signed a letter of intent on November 18, 2026, to develop the proposal. They include the Midland Development Corporation, Midland International Air & Space Port, the New Mexico Spaceport Authority, which operates Spaceport America, and Starfighters Space. Both spaceports are licensed by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).A route for repeat flight testsThe partners want to use the same stretch of airspace for frequent flights, allowing researchers to collect data across multiple tests. One priority is measuring how much an aircraft’s sonic boom raises air pressure at ground level. The corridor could also give researchers a place to develop procedures for coordinating test flights with other aircraft.Starfighters Space intends to fly the route first if it goes ahead. The company operates F-104 jets capable of exceeding Mach 2 from the Midland spaceport and plans to share flight data with the FAA. Its aircraft would give the partners a way to begin gathering data while the company develops its planned air-launch system.“Federal policy is moving faster than the infrastructure, and the country needs a place to fly these vehicles and prove out the procedures that go with them,” Tim Franta, CEO of Starfighters Space, said.Two FAA proposals shape the planThe letter of intent comes as the FAA considers replacing its longstanding ban on overland flights above Mach 1 with a standard based on measurable pressure changes at ground level. The proposed corridor would give regulators flight data as they consider how to apply that standard.In a separate action, the FAA has sought public input on giving launch and reentry operations priority in designated airspace and on expanding US spaceport capacity. The four partners say a corridor connecting two licensed spaceports could serve both efforts. It would give the FAA a way to study how high-speed research flights and spaceflight operations might share airspace with conventional aircraft.Space launches are a longer-term goalThe partners want the route to eventually support flights to or beyond the Kármán line, a commonly used boundary between Earth’s atmosphere and space. They envision using the corridor for suborbital and orbital launches, point-to-point spaceflight, and the return and recovery of vehicles and payloads. The partners argue that linking two inland spaceports could expand the options for launching and recovering spacecraft within the US.Starfighters Space is developing a system that would launch payloads from an aircraft in flight. The company said that system could eventually use the route for suborbital and orbital missions. For now, the letter records the partners’ intent to develop the corridor. The first flights the group has proposed would use Starfighters’ existing jets to collect data for regulators, while launch and recovery remain longer-term goals.

title: Tesla Model Y could carry 7 people as Tesla looks beyond Cybercab
content: Tesla plans to build a driverless Model Y without a steering wheel or pedals to carry groups too large for its two-seat Cybercab. CEO Elon Musk outlined the proposal on November 18 while speaking from China at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit.Musk said the SUV could carry six or seven people, giving families a way to travel together on Tesla’s Robotaxi service. He gave no launch date, price or production location for the vehicle.Where the Cybercab falls shortThe proposal came up when DealBook host Andrew Ross Sorkin asked whether Tesla would eventually stop selling conventional cars as it shifts Cybertruck production capacity toward the Cybercab. Musk defended the Cybercab’s two-seat layout, saying cars carry an average of about 1.2 people and that a two-seater could cover roughly 90 percent of passenger miles.“We still need autonomous vehicles if you’ve got 4 or 6, or a whole family,” Musk said. Tesla already uses Model Ys in its Robotaxi fleet, with vehicles operating around the clock in eight cities, according to reports.Those SUVs retain their steering wheels and pedals. The proposed Model Y would give the service a larger vehicle designed to operate without either.Three-row SUV already on saleTesla already sells a longer version of the SUV. The Model Y L, which seats six across three rows, launched in China in August 2025 and went on sale in the US in July at $61,990.Musk once suggested advances in self-driving could keep the longer SUV out of America. Tesla has also offered a seven-seat option on the standard Model Y. Musk did not specify which version would underpin the driverless vehicle.Sorkin said he had ordered a Model Y L for his family and was still waiting for it. Musk called it Tesla’s most popular car and suggested the company might eventually shift all Model Y production to the longer version. “It’s what most people seem to want,” Musk said. He announced no change to Tesla’s production lines.Buyers want option to driveTesla has begun inviting select customers to buy the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, with deliveries targeted for December. According to reports, the Cybercab requires a $299 monthly subscription to operate and can drive only within Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas.The company has yet to provide details about where the proposed Model Y could operate or whether customers would be able to buy one.Cox Automotive’s 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Study found that just 10 percent of US respondents chose fully driverless Level 5 as the most appealing option for a vehicle they would own, down from 17 percent in 2016.The most popular choice, at 28%, was Level 4 as described in the survey, which would let the vehicle drive itself while preserving the option for a person to take over.Tesla is already expanding the Cybercab’s reach as a ride-hailing vehicle. The service launched Cybercab rides in Austin in September and expanded them to Dallas on November 19, according to reports.The larger Model Y would address a different need by letting families and other groups book a single ride.

title: Harvard’s two-layer flat lens uses nanoscale pillars to cut light loss
content: Normal antireflection coatings cut glare on smooth, even surfaces, but don’t work well on metasurfaces.Now, researchers at Harvard SEAS have developed a new bilayer metasurface with a built-in antireflective coating to boost the efficiency of optical devices.Smartphone cameras use flat, ultra-thin “metalenses” rather than curved glass to focus images and sense depth. Unfortunately, these devices suffer from lost light as unwanted reflections bounce incoming rays away before they reach the sensor.Harvard team just solved this problem. Led by applied physics professor Federico Capasso, the team created this bilayer metasurface that promises to supercharge optical efficiency across consumer and scientific tech.An electron microscope image of an antireflective bilayer metasurface engineered by the Harvard team. Credit: Capasso group at Harvard SEASStacked nanostructuresUsual antireflective coatings fail on metasurfaces. While a metalens looks smooth to the naked eye, it is actually covered in millions of microscopic pillars of varying sizes. Each pillar slows light down at a slightly different rate, meaning a one-size-fits-all coating cannot stop reflections across the entire surface.Harvard’s solution stacks two layers of freestanding titanium dioxide nanostructures directly on top of one another. Co-first author and graduate student Davide Cassara explained that the upper pillar is specifically designed to match the exact geometry of the pillar beneath it. This design pattern creates customized, point-by-point reflection control across the entire lens.“Antireflection coatings are widely used in technology to minimize residual reflections that are detrimental to device performance,” Capasso said. “The work we have done here is a first application for bilayer metasurfaces that we expect will lead to a wide-ranging impact in photonics.”Stopping light loss is only the beginning. Adding a second, independently shaped layer unlocks massive new design freedom for optical engineers. Researchers tested this design using a free-standing titanium dioxide metalens operating at a 1,310 nm wavelength. According to the study, the metalens achieved sharp focusing and even reduced reflections below those of bare glass. These results confirm that bilayer metasurfaces can simultaneously shape light and suppress glare at the nanoscale.Stopping light loss at the nanoscaleFuture multilayer lenses could manipulate light polarization, eliminate color distortion for crystal-clear imaging, or even trap cold atoms inside quantum computers. The design framework could eventually expand beyond titanium dioxide to other powerhouse materials like silicon.Major tech players are already taking notice. The project stems from a long-running partnership with Corning Incorporated, a leader in glass and optical physics, backed by funding from the National Science Foundation and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research.“This research with Harvard showcases the value of long-term collaborations between academia and industry as well as the importance of combining materials science and engineering expertise to real-world product advancements,” said Paulo Dainese, Senior Principal Scientist, Corning. “By combining Corning and Harvard’s deep expertise in optical physics, this research has the potential to drive advancements in optical lens technology across multiple industries.”With Harvard’s Office of Technology Development actively pursuing commercialization, these microscopic double-decker lenses could soon power the next generation of lightweight AR/VR headsets, sharper facial recognition, and advanced medical imaging.

title: Thales links sensors, weapons in live test of modular air defense system
content: French defense company Thales has carried out another live test of its ACE system, designed to improve how the British Army coordinates its forces and responds to battlefield threats.The lightweight command-and-control system serves as the digital backbone of ForceShield UK, an initiative aimed at improving the country’s air defense capabilities.Its modular architecture is designed to integrate existing and future military platforms, sensors, and weapons systems. The latest demonstration highlights Thales’ efforts to develop an adaptable air defense network capable of responding to evolving battlefield threats while supporting the UK’s long-term military modernization plans.Digital defense networkThales has conducted another live demonstration of its Agile C4I at The Edge (ACE) system, a digital command-and-control platform designed to help the British Army coordinate its forces and respond to emerging battlefield threats.The lightweight system forms the digital backbone of ForceShield UK, an initiative aimed at strengthening the country’s short-range air defense (SHORAD) capabilities. It connects military equipment, sensors, and weapons systems through a common digital architecture, allowing forces to share information and coordinate responses more effectively.At the heart of ACE is an open, modular architecture that lets forces add new technologies and capabilities without requiring an entirely new system. This approach is intended to help the military upgrade existing equipment, integrate newer technologies, and adapt its capabilities as battlefield requirements change.According to the firm, rather than replacing existing military assets, ACE is designed to improve how they work together. Its architecture can support the integration of different platforms, sensors, and effectors, giving military planners greater flexibility when selecting equipment to address specific threats. The company says ACE can accommodate both existing and future military platforms, sensors, and effectors.Sensors provide information about potential threats, while effectors are the systems used to engage them. Platforms provide the physical systems on which these technologies operate. By bringing these components together through a common digital framework, ACE is intended to improve coordination between different parts of the air defense network.Britain’s defense upgradeThales also plans to integrate additional sensors and effectors into the system through collaborative demonstrations with industry partners. This would allow the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) to evaluate and incorporate different technologies as operational requirements evolve.The company’s latest live demonstration follows earlier efforts to demonstrate the system’s capabilities. These tests are intended to show how ACE can support the integration of different technologies and provide a flexible foundation for future upgrades.ACE is a key component of ForceShield UK, which is intended to provide a long-term approach to strengthening Britain’s air defense capabilities. The program is aligned with the British Army’s 20/40/40 vision, which outlines an approach to balancing traditional military equipment with autonomous systems and other emerging technologies.ForceShield is a modular, multi-layered air defense system within the SkyDefender network, designed to counter evolving aerial threats. It integrates counter-drone (C-UAS) capabilities to protect civilians, military forces, and critical infrastructure from low-altitude threats, including hostile drones. The system combines sensors, command-and-control technology, weapons, and communications in different configurations.Thales says the ForceShield UK program will also follow an industrial partnership model, supporting jobs and expertise across the country’s defense sector. The company estimates that the initiative will sustain more than 1,000 jobs across Northern Ireland and southwest England, in addition to supporting direct and indirect employment throughout the wider UK supply chain.For the British Army, the modular approach behind ACE could offer a way to introduce new technologies into existing defense networks without having to replace the entire infrastructure each time a new capability becomes available.
