title: Electric aircraft reaches 17,200 feet on solid-state batteries with 64% charge left
content: Heavy batteries have kept electric planes from flying higher, but things are moving forward to change that.Helios Horizon, a nonprofit aviation initiative, has wrapped up a milestone flight test campaign that proves solid-state batteries can power sustained, high-altitude flight. On a standout test flight, founder and test pilot Miguel Iturmendi took the aircraft to 17,200 feet and used only 36 percent of its battery power.The feat did more than prove a concept. The flight claimed to break three world records for electric planes under 500 kilograms (1,102 pounds). These included total altitude, horizontal flight altitude, and time to climb past 3,000 meters (9842 feet), which Iturmendi hit in just 27 minutes.“With the higher energy density and greater safety of solid-state batteries, electrification is no longer a limiting factor in aviation; it is a viable enabler of new missions,” Iturmendi said. “I can fly much higher, much longer and at a much lower cost using electrification than I could with an internal-combustion engine on the same airframe.”UND’s hypobaric pressure chamber housed in Odegard Hall helped Helios Horizon test their flight suits. Image courtesy of James DarcyFlying higher Iturmendi is no stranger to pushing the edge of the atmosphere. His test-piloting resume includes stints with Solar Impulse 2, HondaJet, NASA, and the Perlan Project, where he piloted a engineless glider to 66,000 feet. In May, he made history again with what the team described as the “first flight of a human-piloted aircraft powered exclusively by solid-state batteries.”To prepare for even thinner air, Helios Horizon partnered with the University of North Dakota’s John D. Odegard School of Aerospace Sciences. The aircraft carried an experimental gas analyzer built by atmospheric researcher Shawn Wagner during the test campaign. Iturmendi also used the university’s hypobaric chamber to test pressure suits and life support gear.Reportedly, rather than building an airplane from scratch, the team is flying a heavily modified Pipistrel Taurus, a lightweight, two-seat motorized glider. Its sleek, long-winged design maximizes aerodynamic efficiency, making it ideal for climbing through thin, high-altitude air.Helios Horizon’s new solid-state cells deliver about 410 watt-hours per kilogram, marking a 60% jump in energy density over the 260 Wh/kg lithium-ion batteries the team previously used. This advancement in power storage gives the aircraft the extra punch needed to climb higher without weighing down the airframe.A National Aeronautic Association observer witnessed the feats, which are now awaiting official validation from the World Air Sports Federation.Stratospheric space tourismHigher altitudes are already on the calendar. Next, engineers will equip the aircraft with upgraded solid-state batteries that offer 25 percent more energy density. This modification aims to propel the plane past 40,000 feet in early 2027, pushing it higher than typical commercial airliners.For his next commercial venture, Iturmendi plans to build Helios Horizon 2, a pressurized plane designed to regularly carry a pilot and two passengers up to 80,000 feet. Designed for convenience, this glider-inspired plane will be compact enough to transport in a trailer and easy to recharge with standard AC power.This high-altitude capability opens the door for practical uses like atmospheric sensing and reconnaissance, alongside an exciting new frontier in stratospheric tourism. Iturmendi noted that everyday passengers will eventually be able to take the flight and look out the window to see the curvature of the Earth beneath the blackness of space.

title: Major US banks face cyberattack involving 16,000 customer details
content: JPMorgan Chase is investigating a cyberattack involving its external service providers after hackers allegedly accessed marketing records containing customer information. The incident raises concerns about how financial institutions protect data entrusted to outside companies.The bank said its investigation points to unauthorized access to marketing information held by third-party vendors. The exposed records may include customer names and email addresses. JPMorgan plans to contact affected customers directly.A spokesperson stressed that the security incident had no connection to the transaction processing problems reported earlier this week. Those disruptions resulted from a software bug that also affected other U.S. banks.Hackers claim customer dataA cyber extortion group called n0n claimed responsibility for obtaining cardmember engagement records on November 16. According to screenshots reviewed by Reuters, the group claimed access to hundreds of thousands of marketing campaign interactions.The published material reportedly covered tens of thousands of distinct customer email addresses. The report identified more than 16,000 purported customer email addresses in the data. Some records also contained phone numbers and postal codes. The material included approximately 124 bank employee email addresses.The incident also raises questions about how banks manage information shared with external providers. These vendors often handle customer engagement and marketing operations. Their access to sensitive information can create additional security risks.Visa and Mastercard affectedThe same hacking group also published claims involving Visa and Mastercard. Both payment companies acknowledged separate incidents involving third-party providers.Visa said its incident involved a service provider in the Asia-Pacific region. The company stressed that its internal systems remained unaffected. No payment information, including card numbers, was exposed.The data attributed to Visa reportedly covered customers across Hong Kong, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Australia. Published records included purported email addresses, phone numbers and marketing campaign information.Mastercard also confirmed an incident involving an external provider. The company said attackers exposed a limited number of email addresses belonging to customers enrolled in a specific benefits program.The incident did not affect payment information or Mastercard’s payment network. Customers could continue using their cards normally.Banking disruptions draw scrutinyJPMorgan’s security investigation follows separate operational problems across the banking sector. The bank experienced transaction processing disruptions earlier this week because of a software bug. Other major lenders also reported problems.The incidents prompted inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The Treasury Department and OCC contacted banks shortly after the disruptions emerged.Officials wanted to establish whether banks had contained the issue. They also sought confirmation that the outage did not involve a cyberattack.Other recent infrastructure disruptions include a nationwide FAA ground stop and Microsoft’s global email outage. Cryptocurrency exchange Binance also suffered a major hack last month.Cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch says n0n has claimed approximately 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026. The group’s claims involving multiple financial services providers add another concern for institutions managing customer information through external vendors.

title: Google tests quantum contextuality across 105 qubits on Willow chip
content: Google has demonstrated quantum contextuality on its Willow quantum processor, showing that the unusual property of quantum mechanics can persist across large systems and help benchmark hardware.The experiments tested whether quantum processors could outperform classical strategies in several tasks, including a game built around a mathematical paradox. The results could help researchers understand what gives quantum computers an advantage and develop better ways to measure their performance.In a paper published in Science, the Google Quantum AI team reported that its processor won the so-called magic square game 98.3 percent of the time, exceeding the maximum classical success rate of 88.89 percent. The researchers also demonstrated quantum-classical separation in tasks involving systems of up to 105 qubits.A quantum advantageQuantum contextuality describes how the outcome of a measurement can depend on which other compatible measurements are performed alongside it. In other words, a quantum system cannot always be described as having fixed properties waiting to be revealed by observation.The team illustrated the concept using a 3-by-3 grid in which every row must multiply to positive one and every column to negative one. No grid can satisfy both rules because the total number of negative entries would have to be both even and odd.In the magic square game, two players receive a row and a column and must provide matching values at their intersection without communicating. A prearranged classical strategy can win at most eight of nine rounds. Quantum correlations, however, allow the players to win every round in principle.Google tested all nine versions of the game 100,000 times each. Its Willow processor achieved a 98.3 percent win rate, with hardware noise accounting for the remaining losses.The researchers also measured contextuality using a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality. The processor recorded a value of 5.590, comfortably above the classical limit of four and approaching the quantum limit of six.Testing larger systemsThe team then examined whether contextuality could survive as more qubits were added. In a separate Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) parity game, the processor remained above the best classical performance as the number of participating qubits increased to 71.Researchers also ran a hidden-linear-function problem using shallow quantum circuits across processor grids of up to 105 qubits. The system maintained success probabilities above the classical threshold, although performance declined as noise increased with system size.Beyond demonstrating quantum behavior, the experiments revealed a practical use for contextuality tests. The team said the tasks exposed subtle coherent errors that conventional random-circuit benchmarks can overlook.These tests could provide a more demanding measure of hardware quality by comparing a processor’s performance with fixed limits set by quantum mechanics. Such measurements may be useful for evaluating systems intended to run structured algorithms, including simulations relevant to chemistry and materials science.The findings also connect contextuality with magic states, which are important resources for running full algorithms on error-corrected quantum computers. Google said its results offer a way to investigate how this property contributes to quantum computing’s potential advantage.

title: Scientists find brain's hidden speech code that prepares words
content: Scientists at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) have identified a region of the human brain that helps generate spoken words before a person begins talking, challenging a 150-year-old understanding of how speech is processed.The discovery suggests that the brain’s systems for understanding and producing speech are more closely connected than previously thought. It could also help improve surgical procedures that map speech-related brain regions and open new possibilities for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) designed to restore communication.In a study published November 19 in Science, researchers led by Edward Chang identified a small region within Wernicke’s area that becomes active before a person speaks. The region generates a blueprint for the next intended word, rather than simply processing its meaning or monitoring the sound of speech.The finding addresses a longstanding puzzle in neuroscience. Damage to Wernicke’s area, traditionally associated with understanding language, can also affect a person’s ability to produce words.Revisiting a century-old theoryIn the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke observed that patients with damage to the posterior temporal lobe experienced difficulties understanding and producing speech. He proposed that the region contained an “auditory image of words” that helped translate intended words into the movements required for speaking.However, because the region sits within the auditory cortex, it came to be viewed primarily as a center for speech comprehension. Speech production was instead associated with other parts of the brain.The new research points to the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), a subregion within the same general area Wernicke identified. Researchers found that neurons there become active about a quarter-second before a person begins saying a word.This activity encodes properties of entire words, including their length, number of syllables, and frequency of use. Neurons in brain regions responsible for controlling the mouth then translate this information into the movements needed to speak.The researchers also found that neurons involved in hearing speech sit alongside, and sometimes overlap with, those that generate word blueprints. This proximity could help explain how humans learn to turn words they hear into words they can say.New possibilities for speech BCIsThe findings could also change how surgeons identify speech-related regions of the brain before operations, potentially reducing the risk of disrupting a patient’s ability to communicate.The lpSTG may offer another target for BCIs that translate brain activity into speech. Current speech BCIs decode signals from motor regions that control the vocal tract. However, those areas can be damaged in some people who have lost the ability to speak.Because the lpSTG becomes active earlier in the speech-production process, it could provide an alternative source of signals for decoding intended words.In a proof-of-concept experiment, researchers used activity in this region to decode both intended words and heard speech in a person with severe paralysis who could no longer speak.The researchers believe the region’s involvement in both incoming and outgoing speech could eventually help BCIs support two-way communication, allowing people to participate more fully in conversations.The findings establish the lpSTG as an important part of the brain’s speech-generation process, rather than a region dedicated only to understanding language. They could provide a new foundation for technologies designed to restore communication in people with speech impairments.

title: US firm to support development of new propellants to boost aircraft range
content: A Salt Lake City-based company has received a contract from the Department of War to to advance the development of alternative fuel sources. With the $86.3 million award, CycloKinetics will work to advance alternative fuels. “At CycloKinetics we believe that persistent U.S. military superiority depends on airpower resiliency and, to that end, advanced propellants are a decisive tactical and strategic advantage,” said Mukund Karanjikar, CEO and founder of CycloKinetics.“We develop propellants that materially impact the range, payload, speed, and trajectory of both current and future aircraft, missiles, and rockets.” Advanced, drop-in replacement fuels and propellantsThe latest contract will support the development of advanced, high-performance propellants designed to enhance aircraft range, missile capabilities and space launch performance.CycloKinetics specializes in developing advanced, drop-in replacement fuels and propellants for aerospace and defense applications. Its proprietary technologies are designed to deliver improved energy performance while remaining compatible with existing propulsion systems.The award highlights the growing importance of advanced fuel technologies in strengthening military readiness, extending operational range and reducing dependence on conventional fuel systems.“The U.S. Department of War’s awarding to CycloKinetics reflects this administration’s relentless approach to improving the readiness of our Armed Forces. CycloKinetics’ fuel performance contributions significantly improve America’s ability to neutralize enemy forces, in the air, land, sea, space, cyber and nuclear domains,” said Gen. Tod Wolters, CycloKinetics Board Member and retired U.S. Air Force four-star general who served as Commander of the U.S. European Command and NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR).The award comes as the US military continues to explore technologies that can improve operational resilience and strengthen its aerospace capabilities.Advanced propellants could provide strategic advantagesAdvanced propellants could provide strategic advantages by increasing aircraft endurance, extending missile range and reducing the need for frequent refuelling.In its announcement, CycloKinetics emphasized that improved propulsion technologies could play an important role in maintaining US military superiority across multiple operational domains.“By recognizing propellants as a strategic advantage, the U.S. can extend operational reach, reduce refueling dependencies, and maintain a decisive technological overmatch. The key to ensuring future air superiority lies in advanced propellants that power existing and emerging aircraft to victory and we’re honored to be recognized by the U.S. Department of War as a partner in this mission,” added Karanjikar.The development of higher-energy-density propellants could have implications for military aviation, missile systems and space launch operations, particularly where range, payload capacity and operational endurance are critical.The next major challenge will be translating the technology’s reported performance advantages into scalable, commercially viable production.As the aerospace and defense industries continue to prioritize advanced propulsion systems and energy resilience, CycloKinetics’ latest award places the company in a notable position within the evolving market for next-generation aerospace fuels.

title: Apple plans autonomous agent to handle tasks across its devices
content: Apple is developing an autonomous assistant designed to carry out tasks on users’ behalf, marking a push into a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.The proposed system would go beyond answering questions or responding to individual commands. It is being designed to control devices, work across applications and browsers, and coordinate multiple agents to complete tasks.Bloomberg reported on November 20 that Apple outlined its plans in job listings published on its website this week. One listing seeks a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic assistant capable of writing code, browsing the web, controlling apps and navigating devices on a user’s behalf.The system is also expected to handle multistep tasks across browsers and terminals while coordinating specialised sub-agents. Apple is prioritising privacy as it develops the technology, according to the report.Moving beyond Siri’s limitsThe development signals Apple’s ambition to make its assistant more proactive and capable of completing tasks independently.Rather than requiring users to manage each step, the proposed agent could coordinate actions across different applications and tools. Its ability to navigate devices and handle complex workflows would represent a broader role for Apple’s assistant technology.The effort also comes as Apple looks to compete with systems being developed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. These companies are pursuing tools that can take actions for users rather than simply respond to prompts.The planned ability to coordinate sub-agents could allow the assistant to divide complex requests into smaller tasks and manage them across different tools. This would give it a broader role in handling user requests, moving beyond individual commands to completing connected actions across software and devices.The report points to a potential late-2027 launch for Apple’s system. However, the company has not announced a confirmed release date.Apple’s ecosystem offers reachApple’s existing device ecosystem could give the company a significant distribution advantage. The company has around two billion devices in use, offering a large potential base for an assistant integrated into its products.The proposed agent’s ability to operate across devices and applications could make it more useful for users who rely on Apple’s ecosystem for everyday tasks.Privacy is another priority in the development effort. The system is being designed with privacy in mind as it gains the ability to access applications, navigate devices and perform actions on behalf of users.The report also coincided with Anthropic’s initial public offering. Anthropic shares fell in after-hours trading following the news, according to the summary of the report, although the timing alone does not establish a direct link between Apple’s plans and the share-price movement.Apple’s recruitment activity offers an early indication of its ambitions in autonomous assistants. The company is seeking engineering talent to develop a system that could take on more complex digital tasks, but its capabilities and final release plans remain subject to development.

title: US scales up production of truck-transportable nuclear microreactors
content: A new generation of transportable nuclear reactors is moving closer to commercial production in the United States. Two manufacturing sites in California and Tennessee will support the production and fueling of 1-megawatt microreactors. Their development targets initial customer deliveries in 2028, with eventual capacity reaching hundreds of units annually.Radiant plans to invest more than $380 million across the two locations. The expansion will support its Kaleidos reactor, which uses a factory-built design intended for transport by truck. Its production strategy also includes an unusual capability: fueling reactors at a private facility before shipping them to customers.Two sites, different rolesThe expanded El Segundo, California, headquarters will serve as the primary assembly and engineering center. Radiant has committed more than $100 million to its Los Angeles-area operations. The expansion adds approximately 200,000 square feet of manufacturing and research space.Engineers will use the facility to assemble multiple reactors simultaneously. Its equipment includes bridge cranes and dedicated testing infrastructure for reactor control systems. Radiant will also manufacture turbomachinery and power-generation equipment in-house.The facility has already produced the first Kaleidos reactor. That unit is currently at Idaho National Laboratory, where it will undergo testing. The expanded production space will help engineers move from individual reactor builds toward repeatable manufacturing.Tennessee will handle another critical part of the process. Radiant is developing an 81-acre campus in Oak Ridge for reactor manufacturing, fueling, and storage. The project represents an additional investment of approximately $280 million.Its fueling infrastructure will allow Radiant to prepare sealed reactors before transporting them to customer locations. This approach could simplify deployment for military installations and commercial facilities. Customers would not need conventional underground construction to establish an on-site nuclear installation.Commercial orders take shapeRadiant has already attracted customers across military and commercial markets. The U.S. Army awarded the company up to $750 million to develop and deploy 15 Kaleidos reactors. Initial deliveries are planned for 2028, with all 15 units expected by 2030.The Department of the Air Force selected Radiant for a microreactor project at Buckley Space Force Base in Colorado. The Navy also chose the company to support energy independence at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana. Commercial data center operator Equinix has separately agreed to purchase 20 units.Testing and fuel supplyThe company is also preparing Kaleidos for full-scale testing at Idaho National Laboratory’s DOME facility. The program will evaluate the same reactor design intended for commercial customers. Testing will examine sustained full-power operation, autonomous controls, and performance at operating temperatures.The Department of Energy has approved the reactor’s Documented Safety Analysis. Kaleidos is now undergoing the DOE’s Readiness Review ahead of its planned full-power test campaign.Fuel availability represents another important part of the production plan. Radiant has secured Department of Energy HALEU allocations and enrichment agreements with Urenco and Centrus Energy. It also signed a multiton TRISO fuel supply agreement with Standard Nuclear extending into the early 2030s.

title: US to boost missile defense, new sensor to modernize seeker tech
content: A Virginia-based company has received contract to develop advanced next-generation sensor for the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptor missile. Leonardo DRS has received this contract from BAE Systems.Leonardo will develop the next-generation infrared focal plane array for THAAD, which remains a critical element of U.S. missile defense architecture, and the next-generation seeker technology is intended to enhance the interceptor’s ability to address evolving and increasingly complex threats.Vital missile defense mission“Leonardo DRS is continuing to expand its role in the munitions seeker market through recent wins that leverage both cooled and uncooled solutions at the detector, sensor and subsystem levels,” said Jerry Hathaway, senior vice president and general manager of DRS Electro-Optical and Infrared Systems. “THAAD is an important strategic program for our company, and we are proud to support this vital missile defense mission. Our ability to combine high-end performance with scalable, cost-effective production makes Leonardo DRS a strong partner for a wide range of mission requirements.”DRS is a leading provider of advanced cooled and uncooled infrared systems for the U.S. government and allied nations worldwide. The company delivers deployed mission capabilities across ground, sea, air and space domains. Advanced sensing technologies remain a key strategic focus for DRS as it integrates its multi-domain sensing expertise with secure communications and laser technologies to support critical national security missions, including missile defense, counter-unmanned aircraft systems, autonomous maritime protection and ground combat operations, according to a press release. Advanced infrared sensing technology for THAAD missilesThe new contract will support the development of advanced infrared sensing technology, while the company expands its Dallas manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand for THAAD interceptor seekers.The next-generation infrared focal plane array is intended to enhance the sensing capabilities of the THAAD interceptor’s seeker. Infrared sensing technology enables defence systems to detect and track objects through their thermal signatures, providing an important capability in challenging operational environments.By developing an advanced generation of infrared sensing technology, Leonardo DRS aims to support the evolving requirements of the THAAD programme as missile defense systems face increasingly complex threats.Leonardo DRS brings expertise in cooled and uncooled infrared technologies, including detectors, sensors and integrated subsystems. Its expanding presence in the munitions seeker market reflects a broader strategy to deliver high-performance sensing solutions for a range of defence applications.As the demand for advanced missile defence solutions continues to evolve, the programme highlights the growing role of high-performance infrared sensors and scalable manufacturing in supporting future national security requirements.As military requirements evolve, defense programmes are placing greater importance on technologies that combine high performance with reliable, scalable production.For Leonardo DRS, the THAAD-related development programme represents an opportunity to strengthen its position in the advanced infrared sensing and munitions seeker markets while supporting a major US missile defence programme.THAAD provides a transportable, rapidly deployable ground-based regional missile defense capability to intercept and destroy short, medium, and intermediate-range ballistic missiles in the terminal or final phase of flight.THAAD is designed to intercept threats both inside and outside the Earth’s atmosphere providing a critical capability for defense against ballistic missile attacks. The system is mobile, rapidly deployable and able to defend military, allied forces, citizen population centers, critical infrastructure and other critical assets anywhere in the world within hours.

title: Iowa plans 1-GW nuclear project with 2,100-MW underground power link
content: ONE Nuclear Energy is evaluating sites in Iowa for a proposed 1,000-megawatt nuclear power project to supply growing industrial and digital infrastructure in the Midwest.The company said Project Northern Pike is being advanced alongside a letter of intent with SOO Green HVDC Link, whose planned underground transmission line would connect Iowa with northern Illinois. The arrangement could give the plant access to regional electricity markets, but does not reserve transmission capacity or commit either party to a final deal.ONE Nuclear is targeting first power generation in Iowa in the mid-2030s. The project remains at an early stage, with site screening and technology evaluation underway. It would require regulatory approvals, grid studies, power offtake agreements and financing before construction could proceed.Transmission link shapes projectThe proposed facility could produce up to 1,000 MW of firm, carbon-free electricity. ONE Nuclear says it could support thousands of construction, engineering and permanent technical jobs, and local suppliers.Its commercial strategy depends in part on SOO Green’s planned 2,100-MW high-voltage direct-current (HVDC) transmission system. The approximately 350-mile underground line is designed to run from Mason City, Iowa, to Yorkville, Illinois, along existing railway corridors.The line is intended to connect the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) and PJM electricity markets, potentially allowing Iowa-generated power to reach customers in northern Illinois. SOO Green is targeting commercial operation in 2032, ahead of ONE Nuclear’s proposed generation start.The letter of intent establishes a framework to explore transmission access into the Commonwealth Edison zone of PJM. It is non-binding and does not guarantee capacity on the line. The two developments are separate projects, and SOO Green is planned as an open-access facility for multiple generators and electricity buyers.Iowa weighs nuclear expansionThe proposal comes as Iowa considers nuclear power to complement its wind generation and meet expected growth in electricity demand from manufacturing and digital infrastructure.The Iowa Nuclear Energy Task Force, established by Governor Kim Reynolds in January 2026, said advanced reactors could play a role in meeting future demand. Its September report recommended a statewide nuclear feasibility study and a program to prepare communities interested in hosting nuclear facilities.Iowa also approved House File 2757, which provides sales and use tax exemptions for nuclear generation facilities from July 1, 2026. Separately, the US Department of Energy announced a loan of up to $1.9 billion in September 2026 to support the planned restart of the Duane Arnold nuclear plant.ONE Nuclear said Project Northern Pike would add up to 1,000 MW of generation to the state’s energy mix. However, it has not selected a site, identified a reactor design, or secured a power purchase agreement.The company’s next steps include further site evaluation, community engagement and technology assessment. The schedule will depend on licensing by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, grid studies, financing, and other approvals.For now, the proposed transmission link offers a potential route to market, not a guarantee that the nuclear project will be built. Both projects must advance independently before the planned connection can support new generation.

title: 1,200 mph F-35C makes first arrested landing on 100,000-ton carrier
content: Lockheed Martin’s F-35C Lightning II has completed its first shipboard launch and recovery trials aboard the U.S. Navy’s newest aircraft carrier, USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79). The tests mark a major step toward integrating the fifth-generation fighter with the Navy’s Ford-class fleet.Two F-35C aircraft from Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, participated in the 11-day evaluation. They conducted 34 flights, including 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings. The trials took place aboard the carrier on Oct. 13, the Navy’s 251st birthday.The evaluation examined how the carrier’s launch and recovery equipment handles the F-35C. It also generated engineering data needed to support future flight operations across the Navy’s newest carrier class.Testing Ford-class flight systemsThe USS John F. Kennedy introduces a different flight deck environment for carrier-based aircraft. Its electromagnetic launch system replaces the traditional steam catapults found aboard older American carriers.Known as the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS), the technology uses controlled electromagnetic force to accelerate aircraft along the flight deck. It allows operators to adjust launch settings to accommodate different aircraft weights and operating conditions.Recovering aircraft presents another engineering challenge. The carrier uses the Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG), which replaces conventional hydraulic arresting equipment. The system captures incoming aircraft using arresting wires and controls the forces involved during landing.Ford-class carriers also feature a redesigned island and flight deck. These changes affect airflow, engine exhaust patterns, and the movement of personnel and aircraft. Consequently, the Navy needed to evaluate how the F-35C would perform within this different operating environment.Trials generate critical engineering dataThe shipboard evaluation followed shore-based testing conducted between January 2024 and May 2025. Engineers used the latest sea trials to examine the interaction between the aircraft and the carrier’s launch and recovery systems.Testing covered EMALS and AAG software, along with their shipboard installations. Engineers also collected measurements to validate the F-35C’s structural models and aircraft loads during launches and recoveries.The findings will help the Navy prepare Aircraft Launch Bulletins and Aircraft Recovery Bulletins. These documents establish the technical parameters crews need when operating aircraft from specific carrier classes.Engineers also assessed the stability of the fighter’s mission systems software. The evaluation included initial use of Block 4 software in a carrier environment. Another objective involved examining aircraft support requirements aboard the new carrier.Sean Jackson, Lockheed Martin’s vice president of the F-35 Development Program, described the trials as a critical milestone. He said the evaluation demonstrated the fighter’s ability to launch and recover from a Ford-class flight deck.Expanding carrier operationsThe successful evaluation clears the F-35C for operations across the Navy’s entire aircraft carrier fleet, according to Lockheed Martin. The result expands the fighter jet’s compatibility beyond the carrier classes already supporting its operations.The F-35C features reinforced landing gear, larger wings, and folding wingtips. These modifications distinguish the carrier variant from the F-35A and short-takeoff-and-vertical-landing F-35B.Its stealth characteristics and sensor systems also give carrier strike groups access to fifth-generation combat capabilities. The aircraft can share battlefield information with other platforms during joint and maritime operations.With the USS John F. Kennedy trials complete, the Navy has another important step toward operating the F-35C from its newest generation of aircraft carriers.

title: Perovskite cells made without toxic solvents keep 96% of efficiency over 2,000 hours
content:
Perovskite cells made without toxic solvents keep 96% of efficiency over 2,000 hours
Researchers at the University of Waterloo and the University of Konstanz have developed inverted perovskite solar cells in which every solution-processed layer is made with green solvents. The cells reach a power conversion efficiency of up to 19.1% and hold up well under heat and continuous operation.
Most high-efficiency perovskite cells use toxic solvents such as DMF and NMP for the perovskite layer, and chlorobenzene for the charge transport layers. Efforts to replace them have usually tackled only one layer. The team, whose work builds on earlier green-solvent efforts such as a
Swansea University team’s use of the same GVL solvent
in printed carbon cells, built the perovskite layer from the green solvent γ-valerolactone (GVL). They mixed in 10% to 20% DMSO as a co-solvent to slow crystallization. GVL alone gave films with wrinkles and pinholes, which shorted many cells. In the finished stack, the self-assembled monolayers are dissolved in isopropanol and the C60 and BCP layers are thermally evaporated, so no toxic solvent is used anywhere.
The researchers also added poly(4-fluorostyrene), a polymer that interacts with the perovskite precursors, slowing crystallization and producing larger grains. According to the paper, it also lowers trap density by about 20% and suppresses ion migration. Hysteresis fell from 2.97% to 0.56%, and the champion efficiency rose from 18.16% for the control to 19.1%.
The biggest gains were in stability:
after about 1,000 hours of storage at 65 °C, the polymer-treated cells kept 98% of their initial efficiency, against 88% for the control.
Operation:
after 2,000 hours of continuous maximum power point tracking, they kept 96%. The control kept 85% after 1,960 hours.
Ambient storage:
after 1,600 hours, they kept about 95%, against 50% for the control.
Temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction showed the polymer pushing the onset of thermal degradation of the perovskite from about 185 °C to between 220 °C and 250 °C. The authors say the stability is among the best reported for inverted cells made entirely with green solvents.

title: Stronger interface anchoring helps perovskite cells survive temperature swings
content:
Stronger interface anchoring helps perovskite cells survive temperature swings
Researchers at Henan University, the University of Naples Federico II, the University of Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London, the University of Stuttgart, the Instituto de Tecnologia Quimica (CSIC-Universitat Politecnica de Valencia), Polymat at the University of the Basque Country, Cardiff University, Henan Normal University, Xiamen University, China Jiliang University, Southeast University, Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin and Bielefeld University have developed a surface pretreatment that makes the buried interface of inverted perovskite solar cells more resistant to temperature cycling.
Indium chloride-treated ITO surface and SAM anchoring. Image credit: Wu et al., Science Advances (2026)
Inverted cells commonly use a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) as the hole-selective contact on a transparent conductive oxide such as ITO. The team says that under temperature swings, thermal expansion mismatch between the layers builds up stress at this interface and weakens adhesion, even without significant chemical degradation. In an untreated stack, the interfacial fracture energy fell from 1.59 to 0.50 J/m² after aging, a 69% reduction. To address this, the researchers treat the ITO with indium chloride before depositing the SAM. The treatment increases the density of hydroxyl groups on the surface and introduces chloride, which the authors say lets the SAM molecules anchor at several points, through metal-oxygen coordination supported by chloride-induced hydrogen bonding. Calculations for two SAM molecules, MeO-2PACz and m-PhPACz, showed stronger adsorption on the treated surface.
The best small-area device (7.81 mm²) reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.3%, certified at 26.9%. A 1 cm² cell reached 25.7%, and a module with a 70 cm² aperture area reached 22.7%. After 400 temperature cycles between -40 and 85°C (ISOS-T-3), the treated devices retained 94% of their initial efficiency, compared with 59% for the control. They also retained 95% after 2,000 hours of continuous illumination with maximum power point tracking, and 95% after 1,000 hours of heating at 85°C.
Thermal stress has been a recurring theme in this line of work. An
earlier study
involving a team led by Meng Li at Henan University found it to be the decisive factor in the degradation of metal-halide perovskites. Preparing the ITO surface for better SAM anchoring has also been
explored before

content:
The European Commission has announced a provisional political agreement
between the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union to
simplify and accelerate permitting procedures for grids and clean energy
infrastructure as part of the European Grid Package.
The initiative was proposed last year to strengthen energy infrastructure
and security while helping to reduce energy prices.
The agreement introduces several changes, including time limits for permitting
procedures covering transmission and distribution grids, standalone energy
storage facilities and charging stations. The measures are intended to
address major bottlenecks, with transmission grid projects currently taking
an average of 10 years to implement.
Under the new rules, permits for transmission lines must be granted within
two years, although this can be extended by up to two additional years
depending on a project's complexity. Distribution line permits will be
subject to a one year deadline.
The permitting process will also be digitalised, and permit requirements
for certain small-scale projects will be removed, helping to streamline
approvals.
The agreement further emphasises the importance of public participation
during project planning and operation. Under the Grid Package, renewable
energy projects with a capacity of more than 10 MW will be required to
improve public acceptance.

title: SSE sets out €3 million annual Arklow Bank 2 fund

政策分类依据: 社区效益基金向项目周边社区分配收益，属环境收益市场化补偿
content:
SSE has announced plans for a €3 million annual community benefit fund
linked to its proposed 800 MW Arklow
Bank Wind Park 2 offshore
wind farm.
The fund would support communities in south Wicklow and north Wexford if
the project secures its remaining approvals and proceeds to operation.
Under the proposal, community benefit payments would begin once the wind
farm enters operation, with advance funding also available during construction
following a positive final investment decision.
The Funding would be directed towards local not-for-profit organisations
and could support community facilities, education initiatives, biodiversity
projects and renewable energy measures.
According to the announcement SSE has already secured planning consent
for the project's operations and maintenance base at Arklow Harbour, as
well as the onshore infrastructure required to connect the wind farm to
Ireland's electricity grid.
Once complete, the project is expected to provide up to €800 million in
economic benefits across Ireland, including around €400 million within
Wicklow and Wexford. SSE added the project could support 2,300 direct and
indirect jobs throughout the projects lifecycle, while the planned operations
base at Arklow Harbour would support an additional 80 permanent roles.
Subject to securing its final planning consent, establishing a route to
market and receiving a positive final investment decision, construction

title: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO
content: On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company’s downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials—and assuage concerns. Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating. Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations. As for the broader market’s jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday’s close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis. For nearly a year, as the five-year-old company repeatedly wowed Wall Street and rankled rivals, Anthropic faced hurdles that threatened to derail its IPO. Some challenges seemed existential. In the end, they slowed the offering by only months. On Wednesday, Anthropic’s IPO sold a record $107 billion, including shares from its founders, at a valuation that made it the world’s sixth-most valuable company. Anthropic’s final lap to the public markets, details of which haven’t been previously reported,  shows how demand for its AI models and agents surged early this year—nearly overwhelming its ability to serve customers. The trajectory holds a lesson for its rival OpenAI, which is expected to go public next year amid continued market upheaval. Cash for Compute Anthropic executives started to seriously think about an IPO in summer 2025. Founded by CEO Dario Amodei and six other ex-OpenAI employees, the startup was generating around $5 billion in annualized revenue, about half of OpenAI’s figure. Executives realized they couldn’t rely solely on venture funding and backers like Amazon to afford enough chips to run and train its AI, according to people familiar with their thinking. By December, Anthropic had hired Wilson Sonsini, the law firm that took Apple and Google public, and begun talks with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which would lead the IPO underwriting. Anthropic had benefited from selling access to its AI models to startups like coding agent developer Cursor. Then last year, Anthropic launched its own coding agent, Claude Code, which soon became a hit. By January, Anthropic projected 2026 sales would quadruple to as much as $18 billion (it generated nearly double that in the first nine months). Still, fast-growing expenses from running its models forced the company to push off its forecasts for reaching positive cash flow to 2028. The company would soon face other speed bumps. In late February, after weeks of pressure , Anthropic told the Defense Department it wouldn’t allow Claude to be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous lethal weapons. The department declared Anthropic a “supply chain risk,” threatenin g to cut it off from wide swaths of its customers. Relations with the government appeared to sour further after The Information reported that Amodei wrote to staff blaming the dispute on Anthropic’s refusal to give “dictator-style praise to Trump.” (He later apologized for the post’s tone.) From right: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, former White House AI czar and podcaster David Sacks, Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and President Donald Trump. (Getty Images) But concerns about the dispute faded as revenue from its coding agents soared, convincing many large investors that Anthropic’s singular focus on business customers made it a better bet than OpenAI. By early March, Anthropic had just passed $19 billion in annualized revenue —more than double its year-end pace and closing the gap with OpenAI. At a Morgan Stanley tech conference in San Francisco, investors and analysts lined up to hear Amodei, who struck a conciliatory note. “Anthropic and the Department of War have much more in common than we have differences,” he said. Meanwhile, Anthropic executives told people that they were aiming to go public as soon as the fourth quarter, possibly November . Compute Crunch In the first months of the year, demand for Claude Code was so high that customers were griping over slow response times and outages, and Anthropic was limiting usage during peak-use hours because of server constraints. That gave OpenAI an opening to promote more expansive limits for Codex, its Claude Code rival. Anthropic had been debating its compute needs for years. Shortly after Rao joined the company in 2024, he and Amodei sometimes differed over how much compute they thought Anthropic should secure in advance , according to people with knowledge of the interaction. Rao often pushed back on getting more, the people said . Amodei described the risks on “The Dwarkesh Podcast” in February: If Anthropic overbought compute and revenue fell short, “there’s no force on earth—there’s no hedge on earth—that could stop me from going bankrupt.” Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, who manages the company’s compute strategy. (Getty Images) Anthropic needed contracts beyond its main compute suppliers, Amazon and Google. Co-founder Tom Brown, who runs compute strategy, approached Elon Musk about renting capacity at his Memphis data centers, say people familiar with the discussions. Anthropic eventually agreed to spend more than $120.5 billion with SpaceX by 2029. In May, after Microsoft walked away from leasing 460 megawatts of compute from neocloud Nscale, Anthropic took around five weeks to hammer out a $45 billion, six-year deal for Nvidia chips in Nscale’s data center in West Virginia, according to people familiar with the matter. All told, Anthropic pulled together nearly $900 billion in compute contracts—several within the past year. Anthropic paid the price for miscalculating AI demand. It told IPO investors this fall it would likely need more short-term compute contracts, which are significantly more expensive than longer-term deals. Race With OpenAI By early May, Anthropic’s advisers were considering a summer filing for the IPO, code-named Lantern. They were eager to beat OpenAI to the punch, figuring Anthropic’s stock would perform better if investors heard their story first. When news broke on May 20 that OpenAI was preparing to file for an IPO, Anthropic and its advisers were surprised and sped up their plans. On June 1, Anthropic announced its confidential filing. Days later, OpenAI filed, too. Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao ( Getty Images ). The rivalry created awkwardness among banks led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which were taking both companies public, say people involved in the process. Investment banks typically separate teams working on competing IPOs. Some bankers nevertheless gathered intelligence about their colleagues’ IPO by questioning fund managers briefed on the plans. The company’s advisers also used Claude to prepare, asking the chatbot to quiz them on what questions the regulators may ask after they submitted the filing. Over the summer, Anthropic executives privately doubted OpenAI could beat them to the public market, said people familiar with those remarks. OpenAI had recently shifted focus toward prioritizing selling its AI to corporations, a pivot that seemed like it would delay its IPO ambitions. Founder Control Investors expected Anthropic to release its IPO paperwork shortly after Labor Day weekend, potentially allowing a late September debut. But Anthropic was sharing few details about its schedule. Nervous investors asked Anthropic’s bankers at Goldman and Morgan Stanley whether the IPO was on track. Bankers didn’t have a clear answer for them and said it could slip to late October or even November. Anthropic had other plans to finalize. Before filing, Anthropic wanted to release a cheaper model—Opus 5.5—to compete with lower-cost open-source models and OpenAI’s. Another complication was determining who would control Anthropic after it went public. After years of fundraising, Amodei, his sister Daniela and five other co-founders were expected to own less than 2%, or less than 12% combined, after the IPO, according to securities filings. The founders also planned to give away much of their wealth—including their holdings—to philanthropic causes, complicating their goal of ensuring Anthropic would pursue its mission of developing AI that didn’t harm humans. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei rings the Nasdaq’s opening bell on Thursday as the company’s shares begin trading. (Getty Images) To retain control, the founders proposed a special class of shares giving them collective voting control in most corporate matters. In late September, Anthropic asked shareholders to approve the change by that weekend. It passed with more than 90% approval, say people familiar with the matter. The following Monday, Anthropic then sent some banks a nearly final version of its IPO filing. The same night, Reuters reported a version of Anthropic’s confidential IPO filing containing second-quarter financials, causing panic among Anthropic executives. The documents had been closely guarded by a small group of bankers and lawyers. Anthropic’s executives have tried to locate the leaks, though without much success, say people familiar with the efforts. By last Friday, Anthropic had nearly finished courting investors. Seven business partners, including Amazon and Nvidia, had pledged to buy $26 billion in IPO shares. At the Patriot bar at the top of JP Morgan headquarters in Manhattan last Friday, Dario told JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon at a fireside chat he hoped the company would “underpromise and overdeliver” on its IPO. Anthropic targeted a moderate valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, setting a price range of $70 to $78 per share. Investor demand reached hundreds of billions of dollars. By Wednesday evening at Goldman Sachs’ New York headquarters, over takeout from Gramercy Tavern, the company’s executives and advisers decided they could go for more: raising the IPO price to $83 per share and selling more shares. Anthropic’s celebrations were muted compared to SpaceX’s IPO extravaganza. Some Anthropic employees watched the livestream at the company’s San Francisco headquarters. One small indulgence marked the occasion: The founders and executives wore “Clawd” pins, the pixelated crab mascot for Claude Code, while they rang the Nasdaq’s opening bell.

title: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
content: Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that’s just five years old. What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we’ve had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies—including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic’s success doesn’t mean the IPO market has opened up. “I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic,” Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information. Anthropic’s IPO is arguably mostly a triumph for early investors, many of whom will cash out in the near term (for details on those winners, see here ). For the company and later investors, the offering is just one stop on what should be a long road. Anthropic now has to demonstrate to public market investors that it deserves its valuation. On first glance, that may not be too difficult. Anthropic’s market capitalization is close to that of Broadcom’s (on a fully diluted basis). Analysts expect Broadcom will generate $175 billion in revenue in the year ending October 2027, up 65% from the most recent fiscal year. Analysts project Anthropic will bring in $127.7 billion in revenue for 2027, more than twice 2026’s expected revenue, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Given the difference in their growth rates, you might say that Anthropic isn’t particularly overvalued relative to, say, Broadcom. But remember, Anthropic has a lot of spending commitments in the next few years, which will absorb most of its cash. Broadcom is a net producer of cash. That puts pressure on Anthropic to not only keep its red-hot growth going but also to find a way to turn profitable. That will be harder than arranging an IPO. What Anthropic’s Value Implies About Zoom and Amazon There may be cheaper ways to get exposure to Anthropic than buying the shares. You could buy into videoconferencing firm Zoom, for instance, which has a stake in Anthropic that in the IPO was worth around $4.9 billion, estimates KeyBanc Capital Markets. That’s the equivalent of around 20% of Zoom’s market capitalization! Then there’s Amazon, whose stake in Anthropic is worth around $338 billion, which is about 12% of the ecommerce-and-cloud giant’s market capitalization. In both cases, we’d bet investors aren’t giving the companies credit for these investments. Indeed, both Amazon and Zoom dropped on Thursday! In Other News • Shares of Advanced Micro Devices dropped 9% on Thursday after Wall Street short-selling research firm Hunterbrook Capital published a report detailing AMD’s business relationships in China, including ties to companies blacklisted by the U.S. government. • OpenAI on Wednesday published new results highlighting the growing capabilities of its AI models in chip design, reporting significant improvements to both its in-house Jalapeño chip and Advanced Micro Devices’ flagship graphics processing unit designs. • TikTok will attend a public roundtable with the U.S. House Select Committee on China on Dec. 15 to answer questions relating to China’s influence on its algorithm and how the company protects Americans’ data, a congressional aide said on Wednesday. • Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu said Thursday that Washington’s new rule barring Chinese companies from accessing Nvidia’s advanced AI chips through overseas data centers “will affect next year’s products and services.” • Google will partner with Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin rocket company for Project Suncatcher, Google’s experimental bid to test solar-powered data centers in space, the companies announced Thursday morning. • Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons struck its latest acquisition by agreeing to buy Mailchimp, an email marketing automation service, from Intuit for $3.68 billion, mostly in cash. Bending Spoons simultaneously announced it had raised $1.3 billion in equity via a private placement with shareholders. For more on Bending Spoons’ financing strategy, see here. • Two energy deals that would provide $3 billion to Google parent company Alphabet have been paused due to muted investor demand and market shakiness, Bloomberg reported. • Apple is developing an AI agent that can browse the web, use apps, and write code, according to recent job postings. title: Why Anthropic’s VC Investors Aren’t Letting Go
content: Earlier this week I reported that at least four venture firms were in line to make at least 10 times their investment in Anthropic, whose shares closed up 17% on the first day of trading Thursday. For many venture capitalists and the endowments and foundations that invest in VC funds, the offering is the first step to turning private shares into cash. But some VCs want even more of the company: Sequoia Capital and Iconiq had planned to buy more shares at the IPO, a person familiar with the firms’ thinking said. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Accel intended to do the same, Bloomberg News reported Tuesday. And Altimeter CEO Brad Gerstner told CNBC his firm aimed to invest $5 billion in the IPO. Many of these investors already stand to reap billions from Anthropic’s IPO: Iconiq and Lightspeed hold some of the largest VC stakes, valued at over $27 billion each based on the size of their stakes before the IPO. Limited partners, the institutions that invest in VC funds, and IPO experts told me that it’s atypical for venture capitalists to buy in an IPO—though it may make more sense for firms that hold some public stocks, like Altimeter, Iconiq and Sequoia. “This is a rather unusual step for traditional VCs, as the V used to stand for Venture, because the companies were not yet proven,” Lise Buyer, founder and managing partner of Class V Group, an IPO advisory service, said in an email. “Venture is meant to be an alternative asset class, versus public equity. As a venture strategy, it’s worth an eyebrow raise.” An increasing number of VC firms have expanded their ability to hold public stocks by becoming registered investment advisers, or RIAs, a status that allows them to invest more than 20% of their funds into public equities and other types of assets outside of the traditional venture investment. They’ve also tried other ways to hold stocks after a portfolio company goes public; Sequoia made a splash a few years ago with a fund that both held public stocks and some of the proceeds from exits of its portfolio companies. It’s unclear how many shares some of these firms ultimately received in Anthropic’s IPO. I hear it was difficult for investors to get the full allocations they’d hoped for. (Altimeter got some of its allocation and was also a buyer after the stock went public, I’m told.) What we do know is that the interest indicates sustained enthusiasm for the AI company—even among firms that have already plunged billions of dollars into it. It also may indicate something about the people who invest in VCs: One early Anthropic investor surmised that these firms’ limited partners may think that the stock has a lot more room to grow and may in turn see the $1.5 trillion fully diluted valuation indicated by the IPO price as a bargain. Many of the investors interested in buying more shares were relative latecomers to Anthropic. Lightspeed led an Anthropic financing at a $61.5 billion valuation in 2025; Altimeter and Iconiq invested in the fall of 2025 at a $183 billion valuation; Accel also came in in 2025; and Sequoia didn’t invest in Anthropic until this past February, at a $380 billion valuation. What’s more, Anthropic sold 980 million shares in its IPO. All told, there will be over 18 billion fully diluted shares, including those representing stock options and other compensation. The size of the offering could be another reason investors are looking for more shares, as the IPO could dilute their ownership. Few, if any, VC firms were expected to sell on Thursday, given a staggered lockup schedule that initially only allows some current and former employees, executives and non-founder directors to sell a slice of their shares on the first trading day. By the time VCs can sell parts of their holdings—which could happen as early as December, but many face limitations until mid to late next year—the stock could have risen well beyond current levels. “Of the investors who will have some of their shares released early, not everybody is going to behave the same,” Jay Ritter, the director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida, said. In other news … Since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last Wednesday, a number of venture capitalists have endorsed a petition to bring Huang back. Stand With Jensen, a petition now signed by over 200,000 people, has among its signees: Sequoia partner Alfred Lin, one of the firm’s co-stewards, and partners Konstantine Buhler and Shaun Maguire; Atreides Management Managing Partner Gavin Baker and and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, we’ve confirmed. Investment firms like Atreides hold a substantial number of Nvidia shares, although they still make up a small percentage of the total stock. Sequoia famously invested in Nvidia at its founding—before the company had made any chips—and helped get Nvidia off the ground. Nvidia shareholders could call a meeting of Nvidia’s board and ask it to reinstate Huang if they could gather a group owning at least 15% of the company’s stock . The support from VC firms could come in handy for such an organizing effort, though it would remain a heavy lift given how dispersed Nvidia’s stock ownership is.— Tiffany Li (This article updates Alfred Lin’s title.) title: Nvidia Nears Acquisition of Diffusion AI Developer for More Than $500 Million
content: Nvidia is in advanced talks to acquire Inception, a two-year-old startup that develops a type of AI that aims to perform faster than the one that powers products such as ChatGPT and Claude, according to three people with knowledge of the discussions. The proposed deal is worth at least $500 million, plus “earnout” awards for the new employees, depending on whether they hit certain goals, one of these people said. The talks show how the chip designer’s AI startup-deal machine and efforts to develop its own AI as a counterweight to Anthropic’s are still humming even as the company faces a leadership crisis following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang. Inception’s so-called diffusion large language models, and the talent behind the technology, are supposed to aid Nvidia’s development of Nemotron open source models, this person said. Nvidia’s talks with Inception, which is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, began before Huang departed and came after Microsoft expressed interest in a similar deal. But there’s little sign Nvidia will pull back from Nemotron after pouring tens of billions of dollars into the models. That includes spending billions of dollars to acquire or quasi-acquire technology and AI researchers to boost its Nemotron-related teams, which have hundreds of employees. The Nemotron models aim to give businesses and governments an alternative to closed-source AI from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as boost Nvidia’s work on AI that powers robots. Nemotron users include Booz Allen , Palantir and a range of U.S. government agencies that don’t want to use Chinese-made open source or open-weight models. Open-source or open-weight models are easier for organizations to customize to their specific needs, compared to closed-source models, but doing so requires a certain level of expertise. The Nvidia models aim to keep compete with Anthropic and OpenAI, as the two leading AI developers are designing their own AI server chips to lessen their reliance on Nvidia’s graphics processing units. As part of the latest acquisition to boost Nemotron, Inception co-founders Stefano Ermon, Aditya Grover, and Volodymyr Kuleshov are expected to join Nvidia full-time, one of the people with knowledge of the deal said. All three are well-known machine learning professors at Stanford University, the University of California, Los Angeles, and Cornell University, respectively. Inception previously raised $50 million in funding from investors like Menlo Ventures, M12, and Mayfield as well as Nvidia. Representatives of Nvidia and Inception did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Inception, which has more than 30 employees, gained notoriety in early 2025 after releasing a diffusion large language model, which is different from standard “autoregressive” language models that generate responses from left to right and power products like ChatGPT and Claude. Diffusion language models work by generating a complete answer that looks messy and seemingly random at first, then repeatedly refining it to a final response. Diffusion has traditionally been used in image generation models but more recently has been applied to language-generating AI by startups like Inception, as well as larger developers such as Google DeepMind. In May, Nvidia itself released a version of its Nemotron language model that combines diffusion with autoregressive and other, more traditional forms of language AI. One of the biggest advantages of diffusion models is that they’re much faster than autoregressive ones, especially when generating longer responses. At Nvidia, the researchers behind Inception also plan to adapt their work to so-called physical models that help robots process the world around them, according to one of the people.

title: Why Bending Spoons Could Tap Convertible Bonds Next
content: Since going public in July, Bending Spoons has tapped the debt and equity markets to raise money mostly to buy more tech firms, and to run its growing portfolio. One financing option the company hasn’t yet used is convertible bonds, but that could make sense soon. With interest rates higher now than they have been, the company is considering issuing convertible bonds, as a supplement to its existing financing, a person close to the company said. Convertible bonds generally have lower interest rates than comparable non-convertible debt, because holders get the option to convert into stock, which can dilute existing shareholders. Its need for capital is likely to remain intense. Bending Spoons has snapped up a slew of aging but well-known tech brands like AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable and Vimeo, betting it can revive their fortunes through aggressive restructuring. Its most recent acquisition was whiteboarding software company Miro, completed in late October at a valuation of around $1.36 billion, a 90% discount to Miro’s 2021 private valuation. The company has typically paid between one and seven times revenue, and is currently targeting buying more companies with at least $500 million in annual revenue with a price tag in the low billions. The firm remains broadly open to acquisitions across different areas of tech, but healthcare technology stands out as an interesting area right now, the person added. Bending Spoons has paid for these acquisitions mostly through borrowed money, supplemented by free cash flow and equity. It generated around $250 million in free cash flow in the first six months of 2026, far less than the $2.3 billion it spent on acquisitions. Bending Spoons aims to maintain a net leverage ratio—debt minus cash divided by earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization—of two to three times. It was within that range at the end of June, when its net debt of $4.09 billion translated to a leverage ratio at around 2.4 times. (The company is set to report third-quarter earnings on Friday.) Moody’s and S&P both rate Bending Spoons below investment grade, so it pays higher rates than blue-chip borrowers. In September, Bending Spoons borrowed roughly $1.7 billion in loans, partly to pay for Miro, and in October it raised $1.8 billion through its first high-yield bond sale. Bending Spoons currently pays a blended effective interest rate of around 9% on its debt, the person said, a figure that typically averages borrowing costs across loans and bonds. Bending Spoons’ borrowing costs could come down somewhat as the company builds more of a track record as a public company, or if broader interest rates fall. Securing an investment-grade credit rating would allow the company to borrow money more cheaply, but Bending Spoons would need to pare down its leverage or make other trade-offs, which it isn’t considering doing right now, the person said. That helps make convertible bonds a potentially attractive option. Bending Spoons views convertible bonds as a potential supplement rather than a core funding source, because they wouldn’t provide funding at a massive scale, the person said. That may partly reflect the company's existing debt or a desire to minimize that potential dilution of existing shareholders. Meanwhile, Bending Spoons has raised equity to run and grow the businesses it already owns, and also to help fund deals. Last month it sold $330 million in stock to Berkshire Hathaway, a private placement that followed Berkshire’s $600 million investment in Bending Spoons’ IPO. Issuing equity instead of debt could help the company keep its leverage ratio below the top of its target range. Once it completes an acquisition, Bending Spoons lays off workers and brings in around 50 to 60 of its own employees, putting its own staff in leadership roles. It’s also raised prices at many acquired companies, although it has no plans to hike prices at Airtable, the productivity software provider it bought in September, the person said. title: Meta Bets on $300 Muse Charm to Boost AI Hardware Business
content: Meta Platforms plans to charge $300 for its forthcoming Muse Charm device and offer user subsidies, according to a person familiar with the matter, betting that the pocket-sized AI gadget will help energize its hardware business and draw users to its new personal assistant. To lure buyers, Meta plans to offer a free 5G data plan from Verizon for up to 12 months that would enable faster responses from Muse, its personal AI agent, wherever users go, the person said. Meta has made Charm, which Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg unveiled at the annual Connect developer conference in September, a priority in its devices lineup. The company delayed the launch of its smartwatch to next year to focus on Charm, and leveraged the work it did on the watch to bring the keychain-like device to market sooner, according to the person. Meta had targeted a 2026 launch for the smartwatch, which has been expected to include health-tracking capabilities and give Meta another way to compete with wearable-device makers including Apple. Competitors are also developing hardware to bring their AI assistants into people’s homes. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device next year, a screen-free smart speaker designed with Jony Ive’s design firm, LoveFrom. Apple, meanwhile, launched its $299 HomeView display in October and is working on a robotic home device that could arrive as soon as next year. Zuckerberg said at Connect that Charm would be available to order around the winter holidays. He described it as a “joyful” device that would let people talk to Muse more easily, including when they weren’t wearing Meta’s smart glasses. Asked about the price and other new information, Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” A Broader Wearables Roadmap Charm is part of a broader push by the company to expand its lineup of AI-powered hardware, including glasses, watches, an AI pendant and, eventually, humanoid robots. In an internal memo outlining the company’s wearables ambitions earlier this year, Meta set a goal of selling 10 million wearable devices in the second half of 2026 and reaching nearly 7 million monthly active users of its wearables by the end of the year. The targets highlight how important wearables have become to Meta’s efforts to turn its AI investments into products people use throughout the day—and to improve the performance of its Reality Labs division, which has consistently recorded billions of dollars in annual losses. The memo outlined an aggressive pipeline of new products and upgrades for Meta’s smart glasses business, as well as plans for a new AI pendant. The pendant would give users another way to access the Muse AI assistant without having to reach for their phones or wear glasses, and it plans to start testing the device internally next year. Meta and its partner, EssilorLuxottica, sold more than 7 million pairs of their Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in 2025, EssilorLuxottica reported in February. Meta’s hardware ambitions could eventually extend beyond devices people wear. Meta’s Reality Labs robotics division has been developing prototypes of humanoid robots with Chinese startup Fourier as part of a longer-term effort to build consumer robots that can help around the house.

title: ServiceNow Builds an AI Weapon to Target Salesforce Customers
content: After a late summer rally, the Saaspocalypse slump in software stocks such as ServiceNow and Salesforce has returned. One reason may be signs that Anthropic’s expansion into tools outside of coding—such as tools to automate legal, finance, human resources, and sales functions, via Claude Cowork—is gaining traction with businesses, Kevin and I reported today . Another factor: established software-as-a-service firms are attacking each other with their own AI tools, which make it easier for them to steal customers from each other. ServiceNow last week released a new tool that can reduce the time it takes companies to switch to its relatively new customer relationship management software from six months to six weeks. Previously ServiceNow would have needed to manually consult with a customer to figure out where their data lived in disparate systems so it could be extracted and moved onto ServiceNow’s customer relationship management software. But now the process can be automated, Paul Fipps, ServiceNow’s president of global customer operations, told me. ServiceNow has historically made software for IT teams but it launched the CRM software less than two years ago, in an effort to woo businesses away from CRM giant Salesforce. Salesforce, meanwhile, has made a show of launching its own IT service management software and says it has poached ServiceNow customers. Other big software-as-a-service companies are unveiling similar tools. Oracle has new AI tools to help automate switching to its enterprise resource planning software, as does rival SAP. And Workday has also released AI agents that help onboard customers to its human resources and finance software much faster. Such tools have had limited impact so far as customers aren’t using them at a large scale, said Julie Teigland, a global vice chair of consulting giant EY. That’s because customers must be unhappy with their big software apps and await the end of their contracts to make a change to another provider, she said. “AI will and has lowered the cost of transition in terms of data migration,” she said, adding, “You're not switching overnight your provider just because the tools are there to make it easier to switch.” Then there’s the threat posed by Anthropic. One reason for Claude Code‘s success is that Anthropic designed it to be simple for customers to incorporate into their existing software development processes, said Mal Vivek, CEO at Zeb, a consulting firm that works with Anthropic customers. Now, a significant percentage of Zeb’s customers are in the process of adopting Claude Managed Agents and Claude Cowork, she said. Those tools include products through Claude Cowork that help businesses automate legal, finance, human resources, and sales functions. Anthropic has also launched tools that help customers build their own legal and finance agents. “There was no need for a company to build a user interface specifically around Claude Code,” said Vivek. “With Claude Managed Agents, I think Anthropic saw adoption would scale quickly once they put templates for these other business functional areas directly in the hands of users, making them easier to adopt.”
